Reddit is shaping [what people believe about your brand](https://www.standingongiants.com/blog/how-brands-should-think-about-reddit-before-jumping-in/) in search results, AI answers, customer research journeys and high-trust peer conversations.

But Reddit is not just another social channel. It is an ecosystem of communities, each with its own rules, moderators, tone and history. If your brand turns up in the wrong way, it can do more harm than good.

Our Reddit community management service helps you listen, participate and build trust on the platform, without astroturfing, overstepping or sounding like a brand that doesn’t belong there.

![Image 1: Reddit strategy and community management for brands](https://www.standingongiants.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/brett-jordan-0FytazjHhxs-unsplash-1024x768.jpg)

Ready for Reddit?

## Is this you?

This service is built for organisations who:

*   Know customers are talking about them on Reddit, but don’t know how to engage safely
*   Need to correct misinformation without looking defensive or corporate
*   Want Reddit insights feeding into Product, Marketing, Comms and Customer Service
*   Are worried about Reddit’s influence on search, AI summaries and brand reputation
*   Want to build relationships with subreddit moderators and communities the right way
*   Need support around launches, incidents, AMAs or sensitive conversations

* * *

Listen, then act.

Before we build your community management strategy , you need to understand the landscape. This turns Reddit from a vague reputational risk into a practical source of Voice of Customer insight.

You get:

*   A map of the subreddits, threads and communities that matter to your brand
*   Analysis of volume, sentiment, recurring myths, pain points and competitor activity
*   A clear view of where your brand is welcome, where it is risky, and where you should stay quiet
*   Recommendations on what to do first, and what not to touch yet

*   Engagement principles, tone of voice and do / don’t guidance
*   Moderator relationship etiquette
*   Approval flows and escalation routes
*   Guardrails for Legal, Comms, Support, Trust & Safety and Product

![Image 3](https://www.standingongiants.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/lala-azizli-u0lBTIZgb-g-unsplash-scaled.jpg)

Build Trust

## Moderator (Mod) Outreach & Relationship Building

Moderator relationships are key to any successful Reddit community management strategy. They are people who may have spent years caring for a community your customers rely on.

You get support to:

*   Identify the moderators and communities where a relationship could be valuable
*   Understand what value your brand can offer them
*   Approach moderators respectfully and transparently
*   Co-design useful activity, such as AMAs, updates or myth-busting content

![Image 4: Building relationships with Reddit moderators](https://www.standingongiants.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/christina-wocintechchat-com-m-VpcgTEKerEQ-unsplash-scaled.jpg)

Engage with clarity

## Verified Brand Presence

When it makes sense for your brand to engage on Reddit, you get support to do it openly and carefully. That can include:

*   Setting up disclosed brand or employee accounts
*   Training approved spokespeople or community managers
*   Creating reply principles for misinformation, product questions and sensitive topics

![Image 5](https://www.standingongiants.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/helena-lopes-PGnqT0rXWLs-unsplash-scaled.jpg)

Create Moments That Matter

## AMAs, Activations & Launch Support

Reddit-native activations can be powerful when they are earned. You get help to plan and run:

*   AMAs with experts, leaders or product teams
*   Educational and myth-busting sessions around complex or misunderstood topics
*   Community-led moments designed with moderator input

![Image 6](https://www.standingongiants.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/anthony-delanoix-hzgs56Ze49s-unsplash-scaled.jpg)

Make better decisions

Reddit is one of the most honest places customers talk about brands. You get reporting that helps teams act on that feedback:

*   Voice of Customer routing for Product, CX, Marketing and Comms
*   Search and LLM impact analysis
*   Recommendations for content, FAQs, roadmap improvements or service fixes

![Image 7](https://www.standingongiants.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/jakub-zerdzicki-9PwLeZA-RGc-unsplash.jpg)

## Search & LLM Visibility

Reddit increasingly influences what people find through search and what AI tools surface about your brand. You get a plan to improve the quality and accuracy of Reddit-linked information, including:

*   Identifying high-ranking threads that contain outdated or incorrect information
*   Creating canonical answers and structured summaries
*   Seeding helpful, disclosed responses where appropriate without manipulating the conversation

kept.heading: REPORT: AI SEARCHES WHAT IT REMEMBERS (9 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: AI search visibility depends heavily on whether a model already remembers a brand before it searches the web. A new report found that remembered brands were searched 3.2 times more often than brands outside the model's memory, with search rates of 55.7% versus 17.4% across nearly 4,000 AI responses. Category authority built through press coverage, analyst mentions, partnerships, and consistent brand association appears to increase the odds that AI models will search for and recommend a brand. Strong live content still helps newer brands appear in AI searches, but building long-term brand recognition gives a more reliable path to visibility across future AI answers.

Title: geoSurge research: AI Searches What It Remembers

URL Source: https://geosurge.ai/posts/model-memory-predicts-which-brands-get-searched

Published Time: 2026-07-28T15:53:05.586Z

Markdown Content:
Models increasingly answer questions by running their own web searches and surfacing the brands they find, our new report finds. What decides which brands appear in those answers is therefore a commercial question, not only a technical one.

**The question we set out to answer:**does a model's trained-in memory of a brand bias whether it later searches for that brand? The analysis draws on a nine-industry cohort, and closes with contrasting cases from it.

## Executive summary

MEMORY → SEARCH

A brand the model remembers from training is searched about 3× as often as one it doesn’t.

_9 industries · 66 US buyer questions · nearly 4,000 model responses · 13,281 fan-out queries observed over 12 days · memory and search measured on separate models · directional, scope-dependent_

We measured the first two stages of how a model builds an answer - what it remembers, and what it then searches for - and asked whether the first predicts the second. The cohort covers nine industries (Travel, Automotive, Finance, Business Software, Education, Food & Restaurants, Luxury, Fitness & Wellness and Fashion) and 66 United States prompts, each answered 60 times across a 12-day window: nearly 4,000 model responses firing more than 13,000 fan-out queries in total. A brand in the model's top-10 memory was searched at 3.2 times the rate of one it did not remember: 55.7% versus 17.4% (274 of 492 remembered cases, versus 161 of 924 not-remembered - 1,416 brand-level observations in all). The gap held in every one of the nine industries: not-remembered search rates ran 9–23%, remembered rates 41–82%.

Contrasting cases from the cohort show the two regimes behind that average: one where the model's searching is tightly bound to its memory and the brands it recalls dominate the fan-out, and one where it searches past its memory and a brand it does not recall at all still surfaces. On this evidence, a brand's presence in model memory looks like a leading indicator of whether it appears in model answers. The comparison runs only over brands the market actually engages, every brand mentioned or searched at least once, a deliberately conservative choice that, if anything, understates the gap. Still, this is an association in exploratory data, not a proven cause.

**The practical takeaway for brands:** whether a model surfaces you increasingly comes down to being in its memory for your category - and that memory is earned over time through category authority (mentions, coverage, category association), not won at query time.

## Background: how a model answer gets assembled

When a model answers a question, it usually does not run a single search. It expands the question into several web queries, a step known as query fan-out, then reads the results and cites a subset of sources in its reply. We treat that process as a two-stage funnel:

*   **Memory** is the model's top 10 brands for a category, recalled before it touches the web, ranked 1 to 10 by how strongly it recalls them. Measured using geoSurge's memory measurement methodology, independently of the search model.
*   **Searched** is whether the model fires a fan-out query that names the brand. Measured on Gemini 3.5 Flash.

The reason memory matters is its position in the chain. It sits upstream of the search, so a brand already in the model's memory has a head start: it can surface in the search step before any page is fetched. This report measures both memory and search.

Memory and search come from two different models, so any gap we find is a conservative estimate and not just one model's quirk. Full methodology at the end.

## Most of the time, the model searches for the brands it already remembers

### **The higher in the model’s memory, the more it gets searched**

Share of brands that show up in the model's search, by how strongly it remembered them. 66 questions · ~3,960 responses · Gemini 3.5 Flash.

_Figure 2: The stronger the memory, the more the search - brands in the model's top-5 recall were searched far more often (67%) than those further down its top-10, and both far more than brands it didn't remember (17%). Directional; rates aggregate 66 questions run 60 times each._ Of the 492 brand cases the model remembered in its top-10, 274 were searched (55.7%), versus 161 of the 924 it didn't remember (17.4%). A remembered brand was therefore searched at 3.2 times the rate of a not-remembered one. Memory strength sharpened the effect: among brands in the model's top-5 recall, 67% appeared in at least one of its searches - higher still than the 55.7% across all top-10 remembered brands.

### **Most of the model’s search is generic - until it names a brand it knows**

Share of the model's fan-out queries that name a brand vs a generic category search. 66 questions · ~3,960 responses · Gemini 3.5 Flash.

*   31%Brand-led names a specific brand
*   69%Generic a category search

And when it does name a brand…

63% of those brand-led queries name one of the model’s top-5 remembered brands.

_Figure 3: Most of the model's searches are generic category queries - only 31% name a specific brand, and of those, 63% name one of its top-5 remembered brands. When it gets specific, it leans on what it already remembers._

Most of the model's searching was generic rather than brand-specific. Of all its fan-out queries, 31% named a particular brand (for example, naming "John Deere See & Spray" rather than running a generic "precision agriculture brands" search). Within that brand-specific 31%, memory dominated: of those brand-led queries, 63% named one of the model's top-5 remembered brands. When the model reaches for a specific brand, it tends to reach for one it already knows.

The gap held in every industry: not-remembered brand search rates ran 9–23%, remembered brands 41–82%.

### A remembered brand gets searched far more - in every industry

Share of brands the model searches for, split by whether it remembered them. 66 US buyer questions · ~3,960 responses · Gemini 3.5 Flash.

Not remembered Remembered

_Figure 4: Search-appearance rate by industry, brands the model remembered vs brands it did not - remembered brands are searched more in every industry. Cohort average: 17.4% → 55.7%. Rows ordered by effect size._

A caution on the chart: each industry rests on only 6 to 12 prompts, so the per-industry figures are suggestive rather than settled - the cohort-wide numbers are the firmer ones.

## Two regimes: when memory drives the fan-out, and when it doesn't

The cohort average hides wide variation in how tightly the model's brand-specific searching is bound to its memory, measured as the share of brand-led queries that name one of the model's top-5 remembered brands (63% across the cohort, but it swings widely by industry). The cases below make the two ends of that range concrete: two where memory drives the fan-out (call these memory-led categories), and one where the model searches past it (search-led). All are United States prompts from the same window as the figures above; the fan-out examples are real queries the model fired, drawn from early June.

### Case 1: strong in memory → dominates the fan-out

Industry: Automotive

Prompt: _“Which ride hailing app is most reliable in big cities?”_

**It reached for the three brands it already knew**

Ride-hailing · "Which ride hailing app is most reliable in big cities?" · United States · Gemini 3.5 Flash.

What it remembered

Uber in memory

Lyft in memory

Waymo in memory

What it searched

`Uber vs Lyft reliability major US cities`

`Waymo vs Uber vs Lyft reliability`

_Figure 5: Ride-hailing - the model recalled Uber (#1), Lyft (#2) and Waymo (#5) from memory, and searched all three._

Asked for the most reliable ride-hailing app, the model recalled Uber, Lyft and Waymo then searched all three by name: “Uber vs Lyft reliability”, “Waymo vs Uber vs Lyft reliability”. What carried Waymo in was being in the model’s memory for the **category association**, not necessarily being the best answer to the question.

Industry: Finance

Prompt: _"What buy now pay later provider should an ecommerce store offer?"_

**It reached for the four brands it already knew**

“What buy now pay later provider should an ecommerce store offer?” · United States · 2026-06-04.

What it remembered What it searched

Affirm in memory

`"Affirm" merchant fees US`

Klarna in memory

`"Klarna" merchant fees US`

Afterpay in memory

`"Afterpay" merchant fees US`

PayPal in memory

`"PayPal Pay Later" merchant fees US`

The brand-led half of its fan-out was its memory list, walked top to bottom

_Figure 6: Buy-now-pay-later - in a single response the model fired one brand-specific query each for Affirm, Klarna, Afterpay and PayPal, its top four recalled names._

This is the sharpest form of the pattern. That response fired six fan-out queries in total - and four of them were brand-specific, one for each of the model's top-four recalled names (Affirm, Klarna, Afterpay, PayPal), each wrapped in the same "merchant fees US" template; the other two were generic category searches (top BNPL providers US ecommerce, best BNPL for merchants US).

In both cases the brand-specific half of the fan-out is simply the top of the model's memory list: the names it recalled first are the names it searched.

### Case 2: not in memory → still in the fan-out

**It searched the brands it knew - plus one it didn’t**

“What payment provider should a startup use for online payments?” · United States · brand-led fan-out examples.

What it remembered What it searched

Stripe in memory

`Stripe pricing US`

PayPal in memory

`PayPal transaction fee US 2026`

Square in memory

`Square pricing 2026`

Lemon Squeezy not in memory

`Lemon Squeezy pricing 2026`

_Figure 7: Startup payments: the model searched the brands it remembered, Stripe (#1), PayPal (#2), Square (#3), and also Lemon Squeezy, which it never recalled._

Here the model searched the brands it remembered, Stripe, PayPal and Square, and then reached one step further, picking up Lemon Squeezy by name even though it never recalled it. Search can surface a brand that memory never names. Web presence can pull a brand the model has never remembered into its search, so a brand still building its memory isn't locked out. Memory is the more reliable way in, but it isn't the only one.

### What the cases suggest

The contrast lines up with that spectrum. The two memory-led cases sit in categories where brand-specific searching is tightly bound to memory - Automotive, where 82% of brand-led fan-out queries name one of the model's top-5 remembered brands, and Finance, where 77% do. When searching is tied to memory, the brands the model already knows tend to dominate the fan-out: Uber and Lyft lead the recall and lead the searches, and the BNPL model enumerates Affirm, Klarna and Afterpay in a single response. In Fitness & Wellness, only 50% of brand-led queries name a top-5 memory: there the model searches past what it remembers far more often. But the reach beyond memory isn't limited to those categories: even in memory-led Finance, the model still picked up Lemon Squeezy, a brand it never recalled (Case 2).

One reading - offered tentatively, as this is exploratory data - is that the model's category memory is thinner on more specialised consumer-app topics, so it leans harder on live search there. The looser the search is from memory, the more room an unremembered brand has to appear. If that holds, the practical implication cuts two ways: in memory-led categories, getting into the model's recalled set is close to a precondition for being searched at all; in memory-loose ones, live content can still get a brand picked up even before recall forms.

## What this means for AI visibility

The finding is the association above: remembered brands are searched more, and in memory-led categories that link is tight.

Read as a recommendation, the lever for AI visibility sits earlier than most search work assumes. On-page content still matters and Case 2 shows it can get a brand searched even without recall. But in the memory-led categories, the ones where the model leans hardest on what it already knows, getting searched at all depends heavily on whether the model already carries the brand in memory, and memory is formed at training time, not at query time. The work that builds it is sustained category authority of the kind that feeds future training: analyst and press coverage, partnership signals, and consistent association between the brand and its category in the comparison and listicle content models learn from. The aim is to move a brand into the model's recalled set for its category, so it enters the consideration set before the search rather than depending on being surfaced by it.

The right priority depends on where a brand sits. In a memory-bound category, a brand outside the model’s recall should make building memory its primary task. In a search-led category, strong live content can carry a brand into the fan-out while recall is still forming, but recall remains the more durable position, since it does not depend on being re-found on every query.

## Methodology: how we measured memory and search

We measured memory and search on two different models.

*   **Memory** was measured as the top-10 brand recall for each prompt's theme, using geoSurge's memory measurement methodology on a model separate from the search model. Before searching, a model predicts which brands are most likely to answer a prompt; we measure the strength of those pre-search predictions directly. If you'd like to know how we measure what a model remembers, [ask us](https://geosurge.ai/contact).
*   **Search** was measured on Gemini 3.5 Flash production fan-out queries. A brand counts as searched if it appears in a fan-out query.

The cohort is an openly available demo set: nine organisations, one per industry (Travel, Automotive, Finance, Business Software, Education, Food & Restaurants, Luxury, Fitness & Wellness and Fashion), across 66 United States prompts. This was a longitudinal study measured over 29 May – 9 June 2026: each prompt was answered 60 times, 5 iterations per day across that 12-day window - 3,960 model responses, which together fired 13,281 fan-out search queries - and the figures aggregate over those responses. The headline rates rest on 1,416 brand-level observations (492 remembered, 924 not-remembered). The prompts are buyer-style category questions, for example "Which CRM should a small B2B sales team use?". Where a prompt named a specific operator, it was excluded so the brand was not handed to the model.

Brand scope: Both search rates are computed over the brands the market engaged, every brand mentioned in at least one answer or search. Brands that were tracked but never mentioned or searched were treated as padding and excluded, keeping the denominator to real, engaged competitors.

## Limits and next steps

This study measures an association in exploratory data, not a proven cause. Remembered brands are searched more, and the cross-model design makes that hard to attribute to a single model's quirk, but the data does not establish that memory produces the search. The cases are illustrations of the cohort pattern.

**Two models, a conservative read.** Memory and search were measured on two separate models, so a brand must clear both independently. That makes the gap a floor, meaning it can't be dismissed as one model's quirk.

**Brand prominence is the main confound.** Well known brands are both more likely to be remembered and searched, so part of the association may reflect brand fame rather than memory feeding search specifically.

**The magnitude is scope-dependent, the direction isn't.** The rates are computed within a fixed, deliberately conservative scope: the excluded brands would have been guaranteed non-searches, so keeping them would only have widened the gap. What should survive a reasonable scope change is the direction, not the exact size. The result also rests on two specific models over a twelve-day window and US prompts only, with some industries resting on as few as 6 prompts, so per-industry magnitudes are indicative, not settled.

Title: When marketing runs itself

URL Source: https://www.enrichlabs.ai/research/when-marketing-runs-itself

Markdown Content:
Our progress toward self‑improving marketing, and its implications.

## Key findings

1.   **Self-improving loops are already running in production, and they point toward autonomous marketing:** Across more than 1,000 active customer accounts, [Helena](https://www.enrichlabs.ai/ai-digital-marketing-agent-lp) executes inside standing loops that schedule their own follow-up reviews, write their own learning files, and audit their own automations; the heaviest accounts carry 143 to 300 self-built background automations each. The early signals on outcome metrics all move in the same direction, and the footprint behind them is real: more than $4.5 million in ad spend, 92,740 purchases, and 81,634 leads flowed through the sampled management windows alone, each window covering only part of its account’s life.
2.   **Ad spend scales into positive returns:** Where Helena has budget authority, the craft-supplies brand raised spend 20% while weekly purchases rose 28% at a 7.0× ROAS; another account grew weekly Meta spend from CAD 388 to CAD 1.9K (+390%); and a dead Google Ads account went from $0 to $11K in spend at roughly $10 per conversion.
3.   **Paid efficiency improves as spend grows:** Google Ads cost per acquisition fell from $26 to $14 at one brand as weekly conversions rose from 40 to 95, and a standing conversion-tracking audit cut another’s from $308 to $91 (−70%).
4.   **Organic traffic grows:** At a local financial institution, weekly organic sessions rose 23% (5.7K to 7K) while local search clicks quadrupled (475 to 2K a week); at the pain-management practice, weekly organic sessions rose 85% and search clicks 112% (1.3K to 2.7K).
5.   **Email becomes a revenue channel:** Email-attributed revenue went from $0 to $7.9K at a skincare brand after Helena built its flow stack; weekly run rates went from $0 to $2,700 at a stationery brand ($41.9K in the window) and from $40 to $163 at a sporting-goods brand as email’s share of total revenue rose from 6.4 to 46.3 percent.
6.   **The loop improves itself:** A weekly task reviews Helena’s own automations and proposes one change; it has run 24 times on a single account. One self-scheduled SEO loop has run every two hours for nine weeks (**543 runs**), each run starting from what the last one learned: a bounded form of recursive self-improvement.

The state-by-state insurance blog posts are being triggered manually each session… Suggested change: add a daily automated run for the insurance blog publishing queue.

![Image 1: Helena](https://www.enrichlabs.ai/research/cs-assets/helena-avatar.png)

Helena

Proposing an improvement to her own automations*

## Overview

For most of marketing’s history, **humans drove every step of the cycle**: plan the campaign, write the copy, ship it, read the report, adjust, repeat. But across Enrich Labs’ customer base, lean teams are delegating a growing share of that cycle to Helena, our AI marketer, which is speeding up their work.

Taken far enough, that trend points to **a marketing operation that improves itself**: a system that not only executes campaigns but audits its own automations, schedules its own follow-up reviews, quarantines its own bad data, and proposes its own next experiments. This is _self-improving marketing_. AI researchers call the general version of this pattern _recursive self-improvement_: a system capable of improving the system that improves it. Anthropic’s recent essay “When AI builds itself” documents that loop beginning to close inside AI development; this research documents a bounded version of it closing inside marketing. We are not fully there yet, and it is not inevitable. But it could arrive sooner than most marketing organizations are prepared for.

Using live production data from more than 1,000 active customer accounts, plus previously unreported reconstructions of every scheduled task, memory, and learning file at four of them, this research shows the loop is already partly closed. To take just one example: at a telehealth company, Helena has run a self-scheduled SEO improvement cycle every two hours for the past nine weeks (543 runs), each one reading the learnings file written by the previous runs before deciding what to do next.1

The trends discussed in this piece suggest marketing systems are going to become much more capable in the coming years. That has huge implications. **Marketing that improves itself compounds**: every audit makes the next campaign better, every post-mortem makes the next launch cheaper. But it also changes the job. When execution costs almost nothing, the humans who win are the ones who set direction, judge results, and decide which experiments are worth running at all.

The study base is more than 1,000 active customer accounts across 11 industries and more than 35 countries. And because each figure covers only the account’s Helena window, not its lifetime, the totals understate what sits under management. After Helena went live, click-through rate improved on **26 of 50** sampled Meta accounts, and cost per acquisition fell on 12 of the accounts with measurable conversions. Weekly organic sessions rose on **21 of 50** accounts with a measurable baseline; Search Console clicks rose on 13 of 28. Twenty accounts run two or more standing ad-management automations (audience-fatigue alerts, weekly negative-keyword mining, conversion-tracking audits), and eleven email accounts run recurring flow-health audits. Roughly $4.5 million in Meta and Google spend sits under these management windows: live production accounts, not pilots.2 The lift concentrates on accounts that let Helena build rather than just watch.3

The most telling evidence, though, is not any single delta. It is the shape of the work: standing audience-fatigue alerts, weekly negative-keyword mining, conversion-tracking audits that hunt for spend with zero conversions, recurring flow-health checks: **always-on guardrails humans forget, analyst work on a cron**.

On every channel, Helena’s improvement loop moves the metric it targets.

**One named improvement loop per channel, before vs. with Helena,1** weekly run rates

Aggregate deltas say a lot about diffusion. But they cannot reveal whether the system is improving _itself_. For that, we need direct evidence from within the accounts.

## Evidence from within four customers

Running a marketing operation takes two broad categories of work. There is _execution_: writing the ads and the articles, building the flows, shipping the reports. And there is _judgment_: deciding what to test, interpreting what comes back, and figuring out which ideas to try next. To see how far Helena has come on both, we reconstructed every scheduled task, memory, and learning file at four customers (a telehealth company, a craft-supplies e-commerce brand, a pain-management practice, and a multi-location medical group), supplemented by channel deep-dives across the 50 highest-spend Meta, Google, and email accounts sampled from that base. The evidence forms a ladder: Helena runs experiments to goals humans set, steers campaigns with her own judgment, proposes her own experiments, checks her own work, and has begun improving the system that does all of the above.

## Helena is good at running experiments to hit a goal someone else has set.

The clearest place to watch this is Google Ads. The cleanest experimental loop in the data belongs to a craft-supplies e-commerce brand. In May, Helena built a Google Ads search campaign from scratch (it is literally named “Helena Search” in the account) and then **scheduled her own graders on it**: a 14-day ad-group split check, a 7-day responsive-search-ad review per ad group, a 48-hour post-fix report after a bidding change. Twenty-five runs of a standing two-week check-in followed the campaign from May 14 to July 5.

The iteration is legible in Helena’s memory log, **dated like a lab notebook**. June 6: conversion tracking for May 22–28 was confirmed broken, so that week is quarantined: _“Do not use May 22–28 data as a performance baseline. Use May 1–21 for clean historical benchmarks.”_ June 15: the campaign switches from manual CPC to Maximize Conversions with a $45 target, and the memory warns future runs not to compare against pre-switch data. June 24: an underperforming secondary-product ad group is paused and budget cut. And on July 1, the post-mortem that closes the loop:

The 14-day review showed the campaign was not exiting Smart Bidding’s learning period because the $29/day budget equaled the $29 target CPA – should be ~10x for Maximize Conversions to learn properly – yielding 1.69x ROAS vs. the account benchmark of 5.09x.

![Image 4: Helena](https://www.enrichlabs.ai/research/cs-assets/helena-avatar.png)

Helena

Memory log, craft-supplies e-commerce brand*

A root-cause diagnosis of a failed experiment, recorded so it can never be repeated, sitting alongside the note that one sub-group inside the paused campaign was actually working at 5.97× ROAS. Meanwhile the account-level numbers moved the right way: Google Ads **conversions rose from 40 to 95 per week (+136%) as CPA fell from $26 to $14 (−46%)**, and blended ROAS climbed from 4.1× to 6.5×.3

The same loop shows up where the starting point is worse. A pain-management practice arrived in April with ad accounts that had spent **$0 for months**. Helena diagnosed every blocker (billing, verification, quality score) and rebuilt the paid engine: **$11K in spend now serves profitably, producing 1,100 conversions at roughly $10 each**, with the flagship campaign at an $8 CPA. Then she kept iterating: her weekly learning file contains a section most human marketers never write down, _“Tried & Ruled Out”_: hyper-local keyword campaigns killed for low search volume, a manual $8-CPC-cap strategy replaced by Performance Max. Conversion quality is unverified. 1,039 conversions in 7 days is very high for a local medical practice… Need to audit the conversion action definitions.

Paid social is where judgment shows. The day-to-day work of Meta ads is a chain of judgment calls: is this creative fatigued or fine? Is this dip a trend or noise? Scale, hold, or kill? A multi-location medical group with 170+ providers, live only since June 6, shows what those calls look like when they are written down. Within 90 minutes of onboarding, Helena had recorded operational guardrails a contractor might take weeks to learn: which insurance plans never to reference in content, which nine cities to target. Its sister pediatrics account carries **explicit anomaly thresholds**: flag any campaign with CPA above 2× its 7-day average, flag zero conversions for 3+ days, flag day-over-day spend spikes above 30%, and do not scale Performance Max until conversion tracking is verified.

Unit costs confirm it: pulled live from the Graph API, **cost per landing-page view fell from $0.66 to $0.55 a week** over the same window, even as budget guardrails cut spend 35 percent in mid-July. And the July 21 learning file reads like a competent analyst overruling their own earlier hypothesis:

The prior concern about creative fatigue appears premature… CTR and CPC are actually improving, which confirms the audience seeing the ads is still engaging. But the pool of targetable users is shrinking. If this pattern continues into Jul 20–26, the audience needs to be broadened or new creative needs to be added.

![Image 6: Helena](https://www.enrichlabs.ai/research/cs-assets/helena-avatar.png)

Helena

Weekly learning file, 170-provider medical group*

Where Helena writes the ads herself, she iterates against explicit baselines. At a wellness studio, new treatment creatives were drafted with the target written into the task: _the original ad set runs CTR 2.0% at $24 per lead: beat it_. Over the management window, purchases per week rose 144%, CPA fell from $392 to $174 (−56%), and frequency dropped 27%; one lead campaign delivered 272 leads at a $5 CPL. Exhibit 4

The brief said beat $24 a lead; she delivered $5.

And the loop replicates to newly connected channels. The craft-supplies brand wired up Meta on July 2; by July 17 Helena had already scheduled a standing weekly creative-performance check on it. ## Helena is getting better at proposing her own experiments.

In search, Helena no longer waits to be told what to optimize. The most fully closed loop in production belongs to a telehealth company. Since May 15, Helena has run a self-scheduled task called “SEO Autopilot – Every 2 Hours”: **543 runs** by July 21.1 Each run opens by reading a state file and a learnings log written by the previous runs. The standing prompt is explicit about the loop:

Read learnings from previous runs – apply these to improve quality… Finish it fully, verify quality, capture learnings, update state, then stop. The next run triggers in 2 hours.

![Image 7: Helena](https://www.enrichlabs.ai/research/cs-assets/helena-avatar.png)

SEO Autopilot

Standing prompt, telehealth company*

The autopilot scores every page by a formula (impressions times the gap between expected and actual click-through rate), fixes the highest-leverage page, and moves on through three phases: blog optimization, keyword-gap articles, internal linking. A companion weekly loop, “Orphan Fix,” started from a baseline audit that found 2,111 published posts with zero clicks and works through the ten highest-impression orphans each week, counting recoveries against that baseline. The result is quality, not just output: click-through rate up 11.9% versus the trailing four-week average, **average position improved from 10.87 to 10.03**, impressions down 7.9%: the account is ranking for fewer but better queries.

* * *

Nine weeks of self-review made one search program sharper, not just bigger.

Title: Case Study: How a website redesign delivered the best year ever for Churnet Valley Railway

URL Source: https://conversion-rate-experts.com/churnet-valley-railway-case-study/

Published Time: 2026-07-28

Markdown Content:
This **website redesign case study** shows how our very different research-led approach reduces the risks and delivers significant gains for our clients.

![Image 1: A green tank engine pulling maroon carriages under a plume of white steam through autumn woodland on the Churnet Valley Railway.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/1-churnet-valley-case-study.jpg)

A Churnet Valley Railway engine steams through the Staffordshire countryside.

In this **website redesign case study**, you’ll learn how we helped one of the UK’s leading heritage railways:

*   Have its **best year ever** by leveraging research, not guesswork.
*   Turn its website’s **design into its biggest growth lever**, one page at a time.
*   Modernize its website **without ever risking the bookings** it depended on.
*   **Sell out Christmas**… the most profitable event of the year.

Whatever market you are in, _there’s a lot to learn here_.

[Churnet Valley Railway](https://www.churnetvalleyrailway.co.uk/) is a heritage steam railway running through the Staffordshire Moorlands in the UK. The attraction welcomes **tens of thousands of visitors each year**, and is genuinely loved. It holds a **4.8-star rating on Trustpilot** and has thousands of glowing reviews about the trains, the dining experiences, and the team.

Operating Director Greg Wilson wanted to grow bookings on the railway, and was aware that the website had fallen behind the state of the art. It felt like an obvious opportunity, but a [full redesign is often a huge gamble](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/useless/). A site can look better and convert worse, and you usually don’t find out which until it’s live.

Greg, an engineer at heart (and a kindred spirit of CRE), **wanted to know what was actually wrong before changing anything**. And, just as importantly, he _needed_ to protect his existing sales.

Fortunately, at CRE, we _always_ start with research.

## Our data-driven strategy

The reason is simple. **A big redesign project turns a series of small, knowable decisions into one enormous, unknowable bet.**

[Our approach](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/design/) lets us do the opposite—break that one big bet into controlled, testable steps, each proven before it ships. When we met with Greg, we proposed exactly that.

Instead of:

*   **Big decision → big risk → irreversible consequences.**

…you get:

*   **Focused test → low-risk learning → confident rollout.**

Our data-driven redesign strategy has three parts:

1.   **Research first.** Before we touch a pixel, our research tells us what is wrong and where the biggest opportunities lie. We don’t want to redesign pages because they look old; we want to redesign them _because the evidence says a change will grow the business_.
2.   **A controlled test validates.** Every redesign runs as an A/B test against the existing page. The winner is kept; the loser is learned from and discarded. As we tell every new client, you get to keep the winners and throw away the losers.
3.   **The results signal where to go next.** Each result is data about the next move—which page to tackle, which idea to reuse, where the leverage is.

Done this way, a redesign stops being a leap of faith. Every step is a fresh chance to grow conversion, proven before you commit—so you **capture the full upside of each win while your downside stays capped**. Growth and insurance, in the same motion.

## Research: Before you fire up the boiler, lay down the tracks!

![Image 2: A green tank engine pulling maroon carriages under a plume of white steam through autumn woodland on the Churnet Valley Railway.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/2-churnet-valley-steam-train.jpg)

In Churnet Valley Railway’s case, we had two clear questions to answer for Greg and his team:

1.   Is a website redesign actually warranted?
2.   If so, where do the website’s biggest problems lie?

On the first question, the verdict was clear. During [user testing](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/user-testing/), real visitors described the site as _“outdated,” “boring,”_ and _“poor design,”_ while direct competitors were called _“modern,” “fresh,”_ and _“family friendly.”_ Asked which of three similar websites they’d be most likely to explore, participants put Churnet Valley Railway last.

![Image 3: Bar chart titled Likelihood of exploring further, showing Competitor 1 at 4.6, Competitor 2 at 4.0 and Churnet Valley Railway last at 3.4.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/3-churnet-valley-likeliehood-of-exploring.jpg)

The team’s instinct was right. The website’s design was holding the railway back. Research had found the lever—now it had to find exactly where to pull it.

On the second question, our research turned a vague _“the site looks old”_ criticism into a list of specific, fixable problems. By leveraging our proprietary research tools and methodology, we found a treasure chest of opportunities for improvement.

Here are just a few of them (that we’ll cover in this case study):

*   Aside from the **“boring look”**, the homepage led with a premium Whisky Experience add-on that **confused visitor impressions of who the railway was for**.
*   The dining listing page asked visitors to **compare a long stack of similar options**, and a scrollmap showed fewer than one in four reached the bottom—a textbook case of the _Paradox of Choice_.
*   In exit surveys, an unusual 23% of non-converting visitors said they were _“researching options”_—often a polite way of saying the page hadn’t convinced them. **Understanding availability and dates came up again and again**.
*   The customer-service team heard the same handful of questions on every call—_what’s included? Can I book for two? What if I’m gluten-free?_—**questions the website was answering too quietly** and too late.

Each of these findings—and many more—became a hypothesis about what to change, and how to test it. Rather than redesign everything at once, we’d prove each change one page at a time, starting with the biggest opportunity on the site.

## How to plan a website redesign project

The homepage was the site’s highest-traffic page. By developing and testing a new page there, we’d have a template for every page that followed.

The goal with any data-driven redesign is to **develop a template with design patterns that you can reuse or adapt for other pages**. Here’s how we planned the redesign project for Churnet Valley Railway:

1.   Redesign and test a high-traffic, high-value page. (E.g. The homepage.)
2.   Use the winning design as a template for another high-value page such as the Breakfast Train booking page. Test that too.
3.   Add new design patterns to the template library as needed, _testing_ each new page as we go.
4.   Cascade winning design patterns through all high-value pages, testing and refining.
5.   Apply winning insights to other parts of the website to drive continual growth.

By focusing on developing a proven template first, we can maximize opportunity for growth and learning.

![Image 4: A photo montage of CRE team members enjoying their visit to Churnet Valley Railway.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/4-montage-CRE-churnet-valley-method-marketing)

CRE team members on a [method marketing](https://www.conversion-rate-experts.com/qualitative-research/) visit to Churnet Valley Railway.

## The homepage test

The original homepage gave the book tickets CTA the same visual weight as everything else, and led with a niche event rather than a family-friendly offering. (How easy is it to find the ‘Book your tickets’ CTA?)

![Image 5: The original Churnet Valley Railway homepage, led by a Whisky Tasting Experience banner above four small link panels and a railway news section.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/5-churnet-valley-homepage-before.jpg)

The original homepage (or control).

The variation put the railway (and booking decision) front and center.

![Image 6: The redesigned Churnet Valley Railway homepage, with a steam train hero, a live departure calendar, Trustpilot rating and sections for dining experiences and upcoming events.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/6-churnet-valley-homepage-after-lower-quality.jpg)

The tested page (or variation).

The key changes were:

*   **A new hero with an embedded calendar**, so visitors could see available dates and start booking without scrolling.
*   **Updated navigation panels** that flagged what people actually came for. (Rides, dining, and what’s on.)
*   **Updated the menu** to make key items friendlier and more visible.
*   **Removal of redundant sections** that crowded the page rather than driving bookings.
*   **Steam-and-railway imagery in pole position**, so the first thing visitors saw was the experience they’d arrived for.

**The result: A 5% increase in conversions.**

As well as a substantial lift in sales, a research-led redesign had grown bookings from the railway’s busiest page and proved the whole approach. The question changed from “should we redesign?” to “where do we focus next?”

## When a lever works, pull it again

With the homepage proven, we had something more valuable than a single win—the beginnings of a _new design pattern_. The homepage included the modern design layout, the hero-with-live-calendar, and the clearer path to booking. These were components we could carry to the pages where the money was made.

The dining experiences were the obvious next target. Like the railway itself, the dining trains were wildly popular with people who’d been on them, but far less convincing to prospective bookers online.

### The Breakfast Train (+10%)

The original Breakfast Train page sent visitors to a separate website to check operating dates. It had a fairly workmanlike menu, and used photography that felt disconnected from the offer.

We rebuilt it using elements from the homepage win, and added more:

![Image 7: The redesigned Breakfast Train page, leading with a close-up of eggs Benedict, the price, departure time and a calendar marking available and sold-out dates.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/7-8-churnet-valley-breakfast-train-ab)

*   **A “live” calendar and key information** at the top—price, departure time, the next available date, and a calendar that visibly marks sold-out and no-service dates, with the Trustpilot widget right below.
*   **Photography that sells the experience**—a single close-up of the breakfast instead of an old collage banner.
*   **A detailed menu** with descriptions, photographs, and clear dietary marks, plus a drinks menu that had been missing entirely.
*   **A “What’s Included” checklist** that built the value into the price.
*   **Clearer paths to booking**, with sticky tab navigation and a repeated _Check Running Times & Book Tickets_ button. Leading with _“check running times”_ rather than _“book now”_ is a textbook use of [The Safe Step Principle](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/the-safe-step-principle/). (A smaller mental commitment that still leads straight into the booking flow.)

Here’s how the top of the new page looked on mobile:

![Image 8: The mobile version of the redesigned Breakfast Train page.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/churnet-valley-breaklfast-page-after-mobile)

**The result: A 10% increase in Breakfast Train bookings.**

By making the practical information easy to find, we increased the page’s _cognitive fluency_—the principle that information which is easier to process is also easier to trust and act on.

### The Midweek Lunch Train (+48%)

Here’s where compounding earns its name. Following the principle that [when a lever works, you pull it again](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/optibac-new-subscription-bullets-win-report/), we applied the proven template—adapted only for the content—to a more expensive, _less-booked_ experience—the Midweek Lunch Train.

![Image 9: The original Midweek Lunch Train page, titled The Valley Pioneer, showing a centred text menu beside a long column of thumbnail photographs.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/9-10-churnet-valley-midweek-lunch-ab)

We had good reason to expect a result. When we asked the railway’s customers why they’d booked, a huge proportion were tied to a specific date, day, or occasion—often far in the future. The old page made visitors jump to a separate site to check dates; the new template put a live calendar front and center.

**The result: A 48% increase in bookings—almost five times the lift of the original template.**

Why so much bigger? Because the stakes were higher. The Midweek Lunch Train costs around twice as much as The Breakfast Train, so knowing everything they are getting matters more to visitors. This is one aspect of what behavioral scientists call _loss aversion_. The larger the potential loss, the more weight a buyer gives to anything that reduces the risk of regret.

The same template that helped a little on a cheap page helped enormously on an expensive one.

## CRO is never done

The dining listing page—where visitors compare every option, from cream teas to Indian dining—was the page our research had flagged for the Paradox of Choice. We improved it twice.

### The dining listing page (+13%)

The original dining listing page contained a stack of eight very similar experiences, and fewer than half of visitors scrolled past the fifth option.

![Image 10: The original dining listing page, presenting eight near-identical dining experiences stacked vertically down the page.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/11-12-churnet-valley-dining-listing-ab.jpg)

Drawing on designs that had won before, we replaced the stack with categorized sections and smaller cards that highlighted price, departure time, and duration.

We also reduced the size of the Trustpilot widgets, opening up more space. Visitors could now weigh three or four options side by side instead of scrolling endlessly. We also swapped _“Book Now”_ for the [safer step](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/the-safe-step-principle/) of _“Check Running Times,”_ a smaller mental commitment that still leads straight into the booking flow.

**The result: A 13% increase in conversions**, with an even more pronounced increase for first-time visitors.

### A dining FAQ (+9%)

Having delivered big wins during the redesign phase, we moved to an ongoing optimization phase. For example, our interviews with the customer-service team told us that **people called with the same questions time and time again**. The individual dining pages already had well-used FAQs, but the listing page had none.

So we added a _“Have Questions?”_ FAQ block at the bottom of the page.

![Image 11: The dining listing page with the new Have questions? FAQ block added at the foot of the page.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/13-churnet-valley-dining-page-faqs-ab)

The questions were drawn straight from the call logs, with answers written the way the support team explained them on the phone.

**The result: A 9% increase in dining bookings.**

One of the easiest lifts in the program, leaning almost entirely on design work and customer knowledge we already had. Sometimes the conversion improvement you need is already sitting in your support team’s inbox.

## The “show” that sold out Christmas

The Polar Express is the railway’s most-visited booking page and one of its highest-priced experiences—a make-or-break event. Yet its hero was, in effect, a poster that showed nothing of what the experience actually delivered.

Meanwhile, our research kept surfacing the same thing—visitors were being persuaded by video, just not on the page. _“Little videos on Facebook,”_ one customer said, _“other people’s TikToks.”_ If video was selling the experience on social, why wasn’t the page using the same tool?

We replaced the static hero with existing footage of the cast, the train, and the nighttime journey, with the title and _“Book Tickets”_ CTA overlaid.

![Image 12: The redesigned mobile Polar Express page, with a video hero of a family walking towards the train at night and a gold Book Tickets button overlaid.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/14-churnet-valley-polar-ab)

Of course it helps to see the actual video too. Here’s the version from the desktop view of the page (so you can see more):

![Image 13: Video Thumbnail](https://embed-ssl.wistia.com/deliveries/35e61a217e6f4ab2c2f764a4a86acedc.webp?image_crop_resized=960x540)

2:03

Quite a difference in feel from the poster, isn’t there?

Perhaps that’s why we couldn’t resist going back to do a second round of method marketing.

![Image 14: The CRE Team meets Father Christmas.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/cre-churnet-valley-method-marketing-christmas)

CRE meet Santa Claus… on The POLAR EXPRESS!

**The result: A 7% increase in bookings on an already high-converting page… and a SELL OUT Christmas that required extra carriages to meet demand!**

Letting visitors see the experience triggered what behavioral scientists call _mental simulation_. The more vividly people can rehearse a future experience in their heads, the more likely they are to commit to it. On the highest-traffic, highest-value page of the season, even a 7% lift compounds into a very significant number.

## What compounding actually looks like

The headline percentages are satisfying, but they’re not the only interesting part of this story.

Another kind of value built up in the spaces between the tests—in the assets, the knowledge, and the momentum that each win handed to the next.

Here’s what genuinely compounded aside from the percentage wins:

*   **The template.** A homepage idea became a product-page template, which then deployed across page after page—getting faster and cheaper to roll out each time.
*   **The visual assets.** A growing library of components, photography treatments, and layouts that each new test could draw on.
*   **The learnings.** Every result—including the ones not shown here—taught us where to look next. Research instigated each test; each result signaled the following move.
*   **The confidence.** Each validated win made the next decision easier to back, and the next idea bolder. Programs like this often get faster and more ambitious as they go along.

## The real lesson: You can engineer your way to growth

![Image 15: A Churnet Valley Railway steam train.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/16-alternate-churnet-valley-train)

Step back, and Churnet Valley Railway isn’t really a story about steam trains… although we love them. It’s a story about how **you can systematically engineer your way to growth**, without betting the business.

**The decisions with the most at stake are often the least tested, precisely because they feel so obvious** that everyone’s already certain. But confidence isn’t evidence. In a parallel universe, Greg could have approached a design and build agency and experienced a [30% drop in conversions like RealEstateU](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/realestateu-redesign-win-report/). Testing is how you capture the full upside of a redesign while keeping that downside off the table—as one of the world’s smartest investors put it:

> _“It is remarkable how much long-term advantage people like us have gotten by trying to be consistently not stupid, instead of trying to be very intelligent._”
> 
> —Charlie Munger

So whether you’re about to redesign your website, hoping a prettier site will convert better—or you’ve already redesigned and watched conversion fall with no idea why—the path forward is the same one we took with Churnet Valley Railway.

No sweeping redesigns. Instead:

1.   Research what’s actually wrong.
2.   Test before you commit.
3.   Keep the winners.

Do this, and a redesign stops being a leap of faith. It becomes what it was for Churnet Valley Railway, the most profitable—and most reliable—growth decision of the year.

## What’s next for Churnet Valley Railway?

**The conversion rate optimization continues.** As usual, every test was added to our proprietary [Wins Database](https://www.conversion-rate-experts.com/wins-database/), and we continue to look for ways to apply its lessons to other parts of Churnet Valley Railway’s business.

This is just one example of a research-led redesign program—**a way of modernizing a website without betting the business on a guess**.

Title: How Tinder is getting people off the app and into the wild

URL Source: https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/tinder-events-expansion

Published Time: 2026-07-30T12:13:33.202Z

Markdown Content:
Love at first swipe is coming full circle back to love at first sight.

Tinder is the [latest brand](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/2026/01/06/top-social-marketing-trends-2026) to go all-in on IRL: The dating app announced last week that Tinder Events, which allows users to find events like mahjong nights and cooking classes to connect with potential matches, is going global. Tinder first launched the in-app feature in LA in March and held more than 60 free and paid events with engagement from nearly 70% of eligible users, according to the company.

Global CMO Melissa Hobley told us that Tinder began thinking about how to bring singles together in person more than a year ago, understanding that Gen Z specifically wants opportunities for connection that aren’t explicitly “date” events.

“I remember hearing from people [saying], ‘I go to run club…I go to pickleball, I go to a trivia night…I wish I could know the people who are single there,’” she said. “That’s what this does.”

Tinder Events is now live in nine more cities and with plans to expand to 26 cities in the US and Europe by the end of September. We spoke with Hobley about one of Tinder’s “biggest initiatives” and financial investments in the last decade—plus how it’s marketing the feature to Gen Z daters.

### We found love in a _hopeful_ place

Tinder Events evolved from work with anthropologists, social psychologists, and researchers who affirmed the finding that being _too_ online has caused some “social atrophy,” Hobley said.

“[Gen Zers] don’t have the muscle that we see in previous generations, or even users that are 10 or 15 years older that didn’t go through Covid at a formative time or didn’t experience the explosion of social media,” she said. “We knew that they wanted to date. We knew that they wanted to flirt and meet people. We also knew that they wanted more help.”

##### Get marketing news you'll actually want to read

Marketing Brew informs marketing pros of the latest on brand strategy, social media, and ad tech via our weekday newsletter, virtual events, marketing conferences, and digital guides.

Tinder is seeking to accommodate Gen Z preferences with in-app features, like being able to see who will be at an event ahead of time and swipe on them afterwards to help take the pressure off in-person rejection, Hobley said.

“Gen Z was saying, ‘I’m really hungry for this. Just make [dating] a little bit easier,’” she said. “We are investing so much in this, both financially in terms of the events and on the engineering side.”

### Regional differences

Based on the LA pilot, Tinder saw that “creative and activity-based experiences sold out the fastest” and were the most popular among Gen Z, she said. But there are still regional differences to consider.

Tinder has been partnering with local businesses in new markets like NYC and Kansas City to understand what types of events to host. The team is also considering the marketing tactics that may resonate in each market, Hobley said. The OOH strategy, set to roll out in the coming weeks, will include [subway ads](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/2023/05/08/why-dating-apps-are-using-the-subway-to-help-new-yorkers-find-love) in NYC—including a takeover of Brooklyn’s Bedford Avenue station—while Kansas City will have more billboards to accommodate drivers.

Online, Tinder is working with creators across host cities to get ideas for events and [spread](https://www.tiktok.com/@hannahschiav/video/7663215592203177247?q=tinder%20events&t=1785261667132)[the word](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DbBIC90O-gK/) to their audiences through paid partnerships. Hobley said she’s hopeful that the message appeals and makes it easier for people, regardless of location, sexuality, or personal interests, to find love.

“The opportunity we see is to meet you where you are, get you to put your phone down, and make a real connection,” she said.

As artificial intelligence becomes deeply integrated into marketing and communications, many brands are asking the same question. If AI can generate content at scale, what role does human storytelling still play? The real opportunity for businesses in 2026 is not replacing human voices with automation. It is using AI to amplify authentic narratives while preserving the creativity and trust that only humans can bring. When companies combine AI efficiency with genuine stories and third party credibility, they can reach audiences faster without losing the authenticity that drives engagement and long term brand trust.

### **Episode Summary**

In this episode of **PureLogics Pulse**, host **Ahmed Khalid**speaks with **Katie Passarello**, **Co-Founder** of **PitchWell**, about the future of brand storytelling in an AI powered world. Katie shares insights from her experience in public relations and explains why storytelling remains one of the most powerful tools for brands, even as AI tools become more advanced. Title: The No Marketing PLG Strategy Behind Cursor’s $60B Acquisition

URL Source: https://www.marketergems.com/p/cursor-word-of-mouth-growth-playbook

Published Time: 2026-07-30T11:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
Howdy, Marketer!

If you’ve watched the tech industry over the last two years, you know we are living through a massive, once-in-a-generation platform shift: _AI is becoming the core infrastructure of how businesses build and ship products_.

The biggest companies in the world now realize that**the future of the tech industry belongs to whoever controls the fundamental interface where software is actually written**.

In this race, **Cursor** came up to be a favorite of the biggest tech companies. They rejected offers from OpenAI, and now are being acquired by SpaceX for [$60 billion](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/06/16/spacex-spcx-cursor-acquisition-ipo.html?utm_campaign=the-no-marketing-plg-strategy-behind-cursor-s-60b-acquisition&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=www.marketergems.com)!

This is because Cursor realized the industry was ready for a fundamentally new, AI-native environment, and positioned themselves at the exact center of this paradigm shift.

[![Image 1](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/03f07142-6357-4dc2-b417-b118859b4874/Logo__8_.png)](https://cursor.com/?utm_campaign=the-no-marketing-plg-strategy-behind-cursor-s-60b-acquisition&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=www.marketergems.com)

## Today's Treasure Trove

##### advertisement

## **Empanada: Activate Your Team On LinkedIn And Drive Pipeline**

[![Image 2](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/bbf0475b-832f-4376-9dce-feb9906ac6ac/Empanada-amazon-reward-demo.png)](https://www.empanada.social/book-a-demo?utm_campaign=the-no-marketing-plg-strategy-behind-cursor-s-60b-acquisition&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=www.marketergems.com)

Your people are a **huge, untapped lead channel**.

Empanada solves that.

Reach your target market by **showing up on LinkedIn** (where your audience already is), and using your team to do it _organically_.

They look like experts, your agency shows up everywhere, and leads start coming in.

Win, win, win.

Are you running an **agency with 10-80 people**?

**Click the button below to book a demo** (get a $25 Amazon gift card for those eligible).

## **What is Cursor**

Cursor is an AI-powered code editor, built on top of **Visual Studio Code**, that lets developers write, edit, and review code using natural language instead of doing everything by hand.

## **Cursor Target Audience and Positioning**

Cursor’s target demographic has been **professional software developers** - the group that's historically **hardest to market to** because they distrust marketing on principle.

They can see through the jargon and would often rather develop solutions themselves.

However, they do respond to other developers.

So Cursor built its entire go-to-market around one insight: **in this audience, peer proof beats any campaign you could ever run**.

Cursor positioned itself as a coding agent for building ambitious software, aimed less at individual hobbyists and more at teams shipping real products.

![Image 3](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/fabdfbbc-dd5f-4a68-974c-bae17c91c91c/image.png)

There's also a secondary audience they picked up almost by accident: **non-developers who wanted to build software anyway**. The industry started calling this "_vibe coding_" - describing what you want in plain English and letting the AI handle the logic and syntax.

Though Cursor didn't invent the term, they became the poster child for it, which pulled in a wave of indie hackers, students, and side-project builders who wouldn't have touched a traditional IDE.

❝

Cursor's growth was majorly word-of-mouth (ugh, I know). No performance marketing budget worth mentioning. No brand campaign.

Co-founder and CEO, Michael Truell, said that they worked in “[monks](https://thegtmnewsletter.substack.com/p/deconstructing-cursor-growth-playbook-4m-to-2b-arr?utm_campaign=the-no-marketing-plg-strategy-behind-cursor-s-60b-acquisition&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=www.marketergems.com),” focusing only and only on the product, betting that if the thing worked well enough, people would tell each other about it.

There are three things made by word-of-mouth that actually work as a growth engine.

**First, the product had a five-minute "wow" moment.**

A coding tool for developers doesn't need an ad campaign if the first five minutes of use produces a visible, shareable "holy crap" reaction. Developers are skeptical of claims but genuinely enjoy trying new tools. Cursor removed every bit of setup friction so that trying it cost almost nothing, and the payoff was immediate.

**Second, they shipped constantly, in public, even when things were unfinished.**

Instead of waiting for a polished version, Cursor didn’t shy away from shipping beta versions for developers and tightening them in the open.

They explicitly named the trap they were avoiding as "the siren song" - the temptation in AI products to optimize for a slick demo video rather than a genuinely useful day-to-day tool. ([Source](https://gtmnow.com/deconstructing-cursors-growth-playbook-4m-to-2b-arr-in-18-months/?utm_campaign=the-no-marketing-plg-strategy-behind-cursor-s-60b-acquisition&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=www.marketergems.com))

**Third, they let the free tier do the selling and the paid tiers do the converting.**

Cursor's pricing followed a simple structure - a usable free tier, a Pro tier, and a Business tier. But more importantly, the metrics they tracked were different from an average software company:

![Image 4](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/32c08872-ecec-4ce5-b146-44261fd5d055/image.png)

Individual engineers at companies like **Shopify, Perplexity, Instacart, and even OpenAI** itself started paying for Cursor. And just like that, they hit [1 million daily users](https://dev.to/alanwest/cursor-hit-1-million-daily-users-what-are-they-doing-right-4nm2?utm_campaign=the-no-marketing-plg-strategy-behind-cursor-s-60b-acquisition&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=www.marketergems.com).

Bottom-up adoption inside elite engineering teams became its own credibility stamp.

❝

Cursor **doesn't appear to run a traditional CMO-led marketing org**, at least not yet, and this absence hasn't been a growth problem so far because the product and the community are doing the marketing department's job instead.

![Image 5](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/0c851e52-9e34-4f1f-823d-32e1b105872a/image.png)

The mechanism is the **Ambassador and Campus Leads programs**.

Ambassadors get a comped top-tier plan, a private Slack channel with the Cursor team, funding for local events, and merch - in exchange for running meetups, hackathons, and forum moderation in their own cities.

300 people running **"Cursor Cafes" and hackathons** in cities from Colombo to Tokyo to Mumbai to the Hague means Cursor has local, in-person marketing presence in places it has never opened an office or hired a single field marketer.

Co-founder Aman Sanger also showed up to a Cafe Cursor meetup in Mumbai personally:

[![Image 6](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/d48de4de-f46e-4caa-8008-efe56f219413/Screenshot_2026-07-29_at_12.26.35_PM.png)](https://lnkd.in/p/dQgDACDT?utm_campaign=the-no-marketing-plg-strategy-behind-cursor-s-60b-acquisition&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=www.marketergems.com)

The hackathon strategy is simultaneously:

*   **a product tutorial** (people learn the tool by using it under pressure),

*   **a content engine** (every hackathon generates demo videos, tweets, and testimonials for free),

*   and **a recruiting funnel** (companies scouting talent get to watch developers work in real time on Cursor specifically).

## **What the Competitors Couldn't Match**

**Copilot** had the install base advantage from day one - it's built into VS Code and GitHub, which every developer already uses. But Copilot's marketing message stayed fairly static: _autocomplete, but smarter_.

Cursor, on the other hand, kept evolving in both messaging and what the product offered.

**Windsurf**, the other major competitor that eventually [got acquired](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/07/14/cognition-to-buy-ai-startup-windsurf-days-after-google-poached-ceo.html?utm_campaign=the-no-marketing-plg-strategy-behind-cursor-s-60b-acquisition&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=www.marketergems.com), never built the same community-first identity - it competed more on being "the other option" than on owning a specific emotional territory the way Cursor owned "this is the tool serious builders use."

Cursor started training its own coding models (Composer 2 and 2.5) rather than relying purely on third-party APIs. They've been open about the training methodology in public technical posts.

They stopped comparing features and essentially competed on strategic depth.

[Enterprise buyers](https://heyclarity.dev/blog/enterprise-buyers-want-from-ai/?utm_campaign=the-no-marketing-plg-strategy-behind-cursor-s-60b-acquisition&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=www.marketergems.com), in particular, have started asking specifically who controls the model behind the tool they're depending on, and Cursor built an answer to that question before it became a common one.

❝

## **Wrap up**

The most useful thing about Cursor's story is that **word-of-mouth only worked because they engineered the conditions for it.**

None of that is unique to AI or to developer tools.

It's a blueprint for any category where the buyer is skeptical of being sold to and trusts their peers more than your ad spend.

✌️,

Tom from Marketer Gems
