Title: From tobacco to Tesla, how the subvertising has held up a mirror to some of the biggest brands

URL Source: https://www.creativebloq.com/design/advertising/from-tobacco-to-tesla-how-the-subvertising-has-held-up-a-mirror-to-some-of-the-biggest-brands

Published Time: 2026-08-02T07:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
The recent [spoof Meta Glasses adverts](https://www.creativebloq.com/design/advertising/the-kylie-jenner-optical-illusion-advert-says-what-everyones-really-thinking-about-metas-ai-glasses) in London show that subvertising is alive and well – and brands and advertisers should pay attention. Guerrilla anti-advertising, campaigns that subvert or satirise a brand's communications can have real power and impact, especially when they're more honest or engaging than the original creatives or connect better with prevailing public sentiment.

With that in mind, it feels like a good time to look back at the history of anti-advertising and some of the best subvertising examples to see when it's worked best, and what brands can learn from it (also see our pick of the [best billboard adverts](https://www.creativebloq.com/design/billboard-advertising-1131681) for more inspiration).

## What is subvertising?

The word subvertising is a portmanteau of “subversion” and “advertising”. A form of culture jamming, it refers to an action or artwork that aims to subvert real brand advertising. This can range from spontaneous graffiti scrawled on a billboard to more planned détournement and coordinated campaigns, either targeting the original advert or replicating its likeness in another location

It has a rich history, from the Billboard Liberation Front in San Francisco and BUGA UP in Australia in the late '70s to the Adbusters Media Foundation's institutionalisation of the practice in the '90s and the anti-[Tesla](https://www.creativebloq.com/tag/tesla) and Meta Glasses adverts of today.

## The Billboard Liberation Front

![Image 1: A modified advert for Max Factor that was the first action by the Billboard Liberation Front](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/WMStt4YuJhSJMv36rZzywR.png)

The Billboard Liberation Front's first intervention on a Max Factor billboard in 1977 (Image credit: Billboard Liberation Front)

I'm not sure if it's possible to really say when subvertising began, but the formation of The Billboard Liberation Front in San Francisco in 1977 is often cited as a key moment. The group exalted billboard jacking beyond individual acts of mischief into something more like an organised movement, or even an art form.

The BLF identified key elements for subverting ads in a way that engaged the public. Often matching brands' fonts, colours and layouts, they used humour to parody PR language, crafting critiques that resonated with the public at a time of growing skepticism toward consumerism. Still operating today, they're also media savvy, issuing press releases and media kits to ensure wider coverage.

## BUGA UP's battle against tobacco advertising

![Image 2: Example of subvertising, also known as billboard hacking or culture jamming showing a modified billboard advert](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/sXr5kWyWqeVWPYWHsT7UGf.webp)

A billboard hijacked by BUGA UP (Image credit: BUGA UP)

In the late '70s and '80s , BUGA UP (Billboard Utilising Graffitists Against Unhealthy Promotion) took on tobacco advertising in Australia and won. They hijacked billboards to modify brand names and slogans, often by erasing or adding a few letters. Benson and Hedges could become "Be on edge". John Player Special became "Lung Slayer Special".

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

BUGA UP questioned the morality of cigarette advertising at a time that a lot of people had the same ethical concerns – public fundraising helped cover the fines when members of the group were arrested. It might not be a coincidence that Australia banned billboard tobacco advertising in 1993, six years before the US and ten years before the UK.

## Adbusters shows reality

![Image 3: Example of subvertising, also known as billboard hacking or culture jamming showing a modified billboard advert](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/5SjXGcSnc4QLYkgRat5zPf.jpg)

Adbusters' makes perfume ads real (Image credit: Adbusters)

In the 1990s, Canada-based Adbusters took subvertising to another level. Going beyond billboard hijacking, it began producing "anti-adverts" or "uncommercials" with the same level of creativity and professional polish as a real ad agency. It also launched a print magazine and promotes Buy Nothing Day on the same day as [Black Friday](https://www.creativebloq.com/tag/black-friday).

The group was established as a formal media foundation after TV channels refused to air its 1988 [animation](https://www.creativebloq.com/art/animation) Talking Rainforest. The piece was a response to an early example of greenwashing from the British Columbia Council of Forest Industries that tried to present tree farms as forests.

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=49mUeTWGWBE)

Like BUGA UP, some of Adbusters' most memorable campaigns targeted advertising that much of the public viewed as harmful. In its series of spoofs criticising the fashion industry's use of potentially harmful body images, an image of a woman bent over a toilet bowl in the style of a Calvin Klein ad presented a more realistic portrayal of an Obsession.

Adbusters showed the brand's own visual design language could become even more powerful when it was used against them.

## Brandalism's appeal to creatives

![Image 4: Brandalism subvertising billboard jacking](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/67utbkDhAo8ccJUfSDuyXD.jpg)

One of Brandalism's ads to raise awareness of the climate crisis (Image credit: Brandalism)

By the 2000s, subvertising was evolving through loose-nit collectives with a connected vision running global coordinated actions. Founded in the UK in 2012, Brandalism shifted its focus from specific interventions to large campaigns, and sought to bring others on board.

Professional artists, including Gee Vaucher, Robert Montgomery and Peter Kennard, have taken part with other volunteers in initiatives with specific objectives, like calling out fossil fuel companies and airlines over climate change. The group's often placed work near advertising offices in a bid to get creative professionals to switch sides.

Image 1 of 3

![Image 5: Brandalism subvertising billboard jacking](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/mtyLuautpeTuf7sz2xns7D-1200-80.jpg)

 (Image credit: Brandalism) 

## AI trolls AI

McDonald's got two lessons for the price of one when it tried running an [AI-generated Christmas ad](https://www.creativebloq.com/ai/ai-art/mcdonalds-pulled-its-ai-christmas-ad-but-its-actor-wont-go-away) in the Netherlands last year: the public doesn't like AI art, and it can be hard to make it go away once you've unleashed it.

The backlash to the "most terrible time of the year" was so strong that McDonald's pulled the advert, but filmmaker Jacob Reed and his agency All Trades wouldn't let it off that easy. since AI-generated work doesn't qualify for copyright protection, and AI-generated characters don't have contracts, they used AI to turn McDonald's AI-generated character rogue.

“I could say the McDonald's commercial I was in was an overstimulating mess filled with unsettling character designs, poor visual treatments, and AI effects that bungle basic physical realism,” the character was made to say before eating a Burger King Whopper.

There was some debate among AI critics about whether the ends justified the means, but a point was made. Brands that use AI visual might have to accept a loss of ownership.

> not sure i understand the vision behind this one pic.twitter.com/j1dM3Ms6WL[February 2, 2026](https://twitter.com/cantworkitout/status/2018473632532754892)

See more

AI companies themselves have also been attacked with the tools they created. AI image generation means it's now easy for anyone to make a realistic-looking imitation of a brand campaign.

OpenAI's real-world minimalist slice-of-life billboards for ChatGPT were met with such confusion that an AI-generated [parody](https://www.creativebloq.com/design/advertising/chatgpts-new-billboard-ads-are-giving-me-tonal-whiplash) shared online momentarily fooled everyone (above).

## Everyone Hates Elon's anti-Tesla campaign

Tesla's reputation has taken a plunge over the last couple of years, partly because it designed a futuristic [pick-up truck that keeps falling apart](https://www.creativebloq.com/design/product-design/the-tesla-cybertruck-design-disaster-just-keeps-getting-worse), and partly because its CEO is [Elon Musk](https://www.creativebloq.com/tag/elon-musk).

After the South African billionaire began expressing opinions on UK politics, the campaign group Everyone Hates Elon caught the moment with its [anti-Tesla adverts](https://www.creativebloq.com/design/poster-design/viral-anti-tesla-ads-show-how-far-a-great-brand-can-fall), and disproved the would be Martian overload's claim that the UK was suppressing free speech. How warmly the ads were received showed how far the Tesla brand has fallen.

Everyone Hates Elon showed itself to be more than a very specific niche guerrilla group with its campaign against Meta. After the company brought in Kylie Jenner to show that people who aren't sexual predators could wear [Meta AI Glasses](https://www.creativebloq.com/design/advertising/the-kylie-jenner-optical-illusion-advert-says-what-everyones-really-thinking-about-metas-ai-glasses), the group transformed its adverts to say what everyone was really thinking.

One intervention used an elaborate lenticular overlay that turned Jenner into a skull-faced alien from John Carpenter’s 1988 sci-fi horror They Live. Another poster taking on Meta's collaboration with Ray-Ban featured the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Meta Glasses are already being dubbed 'Pervert Glasses' in popular parlance.

Can real brands learn from subvertising campaigns? They should try to. Creative anti-advertising campaigns quickly go viral, and they can make a real impact. In a 2023 [article published in Psychology and marketing](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1002/mar.21961?utm_source=copilot.com), researchers Erik Maier and Alexander Mafael found that when a specific brand itself is targeted, brand perception, word‐of‐mouth and purchase intention are negatively affected.

Brands can start by holding real values and ensuring that messaging, visuals and campaigns align with them. Subvertising gains traction when it highlights real ethical problems.

Brands that address diversity, sustainability and fairness leave fewer openings for critique. But astroturfing, greenwashing, pinkwashing and any other kind of washing will get called out. Values need to be genuine and need to penetrate down to the product level.

It’s not always about just sharing numbers, though: This quarter, Huffman took the opportunity to voice concerns and criticisms about Google’s AI Overviews feature, which automatically summarizes search results on most user queries. First, there was a [letter to investors](https://s203.q4cdn.com/380862485/files/doc_financials/2026/q2/Q2-26-Shareholder-Letter.pdf), wherein Huffman spun his narrative about Reddit’s value proposition and general strategic direction amid the proliferation of AI tools. He wrote: > As the internet becomes flooded with synthetic content, people are craving real human perspective. We are the antidote to an automated web. AI compresses the internet into summaries. Reddit delivers the opposite: deep discussions, passionate debates, and lived experiences. People don’t want a summary of Reddit; they want Reddit. The letter also said: > As AI makes information more abundant, the challenge is no longer finding content—it’s finding context, personal opinion, and first-hand accounts. Everything online feels flat, polished, generated, or sponsored, so consumers are overwhelmed and increasingly skeptical. We’ve never had more information, but we’ve never trusted it less. And then, in comments around the earnings report, he [added](https://www.engadget.com/2227553/reddit-s-ceo-sure-seems-frustrated-with-google-s-ai-overviews/): > What we see is, 10 blue links has driven tremendous value and growth to the broader ecosystem… from where we sit, AI Overviews has yet to make a similar level of positive impact, and I think that’s consistent across the broader landscape, right? As businesses, publishers, retailers, we’re still looking for that win-win. To add context to these statements, Reddit has long had a relatively lucrative ($60 million) licensing deal with Google, but Reddit is considering ending that deal, according to a Wall Street Journal [report](https://www.wsj.com/business/media/google-search-publishers-ai-content-0fb06e41?mod=hp_lead_pos8) from earlier this month. The report also said that several prominent publishers are considering similarly cutting ties with Google, including The Economist, Reuters, Politico, and USA Today. (Reddit also has a [deal](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2024/05/openai-will-use-reddit-posts-to-train-chatgpt-under-new-deal/) with OpenAI.) ### Ars Video ### [How The Callisto Protocol's Team Designed Its Terrifying, Immersive Audio](https://www.arstechnica.com/video/watch/how-the-callisto-protocol-designed-its-terrifying-immersive-audio) Last year, a study by Pew Research that looked at data from 900 US adults [concluded](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2025/07/research-shows-google-ai-overviews-reduce-website-clicks-by-almost-half/) that Google’s AI Overviews cut referrals to sites like those by almost half, compared to the “10 blue links” approach that Huffman referred to. It’s important to note, though, that Google has long diverged from just “10 blue links” in other ways even before AI Overviews entered the scene. In light of the Pew Research study, Google told Ars, “This study uses a flawed methodology and skewed queryset that is not representative of Search traffic. We consistently direct billions of clicks to websites daily and have not observed significant drops in aggregate web traffic as is being suggested.” A few days later, Google further countered in its own [blog post](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/search/ai-search-driving-more-queries-higher-quality-clicks/), saying, “total organic click volume from Google Search to websites has been relatively stable year-over-year.” That contradicts what many publishers have been saying, though most publishers are of course wary of sharing too many proprietary numbers publicly. Part of the problem is that both publishers and Reddit have historically depended on regular Google search traffic, but in most cases, the current status quo treats being surfaced as one of the so-called blue links and being part of AI Overviews as a package deal. There have been several efforts to change that situation. Last year, we [reported](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2025/10/inside-the-web-infrastructure-revolt-over-googles-ai-overviews/) on Cloudflare’s attempt to update the default configuration for robots.txt in part to try to force Google to make changes. Google has also [made changes](https://arstechnica.com/google/2026/05/google-will-put-more-links-to-websites-in-ai-overviews/) to AI Overviews that it claims will lead to more prominent links out to other websites than before, but it still maintains that AI Overviews are here to stay and that they’re actually good for the user experience and the web in general. The situation remains unresolved, and Reddit’s shares fell [more than 20 percent](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/why-reddit-rddt-shares-getting-154757142.html) after the earnings report, even though the company’s quarter trounced investors’ expectations on most of the basic financials. The reason? Search referrals were “choppy,” in Huffman’s words, and investors are thus concerned about the future of the site as AI tools continue to disrupt the traditional economics of the web. Markdown Content:
And we are back on the wagon for 8 pm EST! We haven't been laid out by dysentery or measles. Thank god. Yes, I am giving a shoutout to the Oregon Trail, but that's where the nostalgia stops. Now it's time for the bizzzzness.

Two things on my mind this week:

**First, I keep getting cornered on the personal brand question.**“What happens if we build up our people and they leave?" I've answered this one before, and I'm going to keep answering it until people stop asking, because the mentality behind the question is the actual problem. Building someone's voice while they work for you isn't a risk you're taking on. It's the job.

**Second, nobody's talking about brand anymore.** I've sat through demo after demo, panel after panel, watched the entire industry sprint toward agentic everything, and not one person has said the word "taste." Not once. I love AI. I live in Claude more than I live in most of my actual tools. But if the endgame is marketing that's technically correct and completely forgettable, I want no part of it.

The stuff that actually differentiates you, whether it's a person's voice or a brand's point of view, can't be automated, templated, or protected. It only works if you're brave enough to let it out into the world.

So yah. Let's get into it.

♥️ kyle

## **Should You Build Your Employees’ Personal Brands?**

TL;DR - Yes. Yes, you should.

I've talked to a few people over the last few weeks about the importance of building personal brands for employees and executives, and multiple times I've heard some version of the same objection:

_**"We shouldn't be investing in our employees' personal brand. What happens if they leave?"**_

I've written about this before, more than once, because it keeps showing up and it still bugs me every time. My favorite line when I'm introducing someone new to the marketing team I’m lucky to ser is this:

**_“After working with this group, you will never have to use your resume to get a job again.”_**

I mean that. I think it's part of my job to teach people how to build a personal brand, not hoard the spotlight. And I think the company brand should be genuinely supportive of that, not threatened by it. Employee advocacy is almost as important as customer advocacy. Almost.

I was on a call recently, and this exact objection came up. Someone on the team had floated the idea that they shouldn't "juice up" the personal brands of their people because, well, they might get poached. I told him flat out that mentality is dangerous. If someone builds a real personal brand while representing your company, and they eventually get hired away because they're excellent at what they do, that's not a loss.

That's you doing your job right.

Oh and, it can't just be one person carrying the whole company's public voice. Everyone should be building something, even if there's a clear primary face out front. If that's not happening on your team, you need to go change the mentality.

So yah... this has been on my mind lately, partly because of a conversation with a journalist at Fast Company, and partly because it's just become a real thing we deal with at Docebo every week.

At Docebo, I work alongside people who have built real audiences. Our CRO, Mark Kosoglow, has a following that most marketers would kill for. Our CEO, Alessio, is building a presence that's beginning to shape how the market views AI-powered learning. Our Chief People Officer, Lauren, is in the mix too. And we actively support TWO podcasts run by employees and it’s all their personal brands, not Docebos.

Then there's me, doing whatever this is every Sunday night.

Personal brand aren’t separate from company brand. They ARE the company brand. When Mark posts about the future of revenue leadership, people associate that thinking with Docebo. When Alessio talks about the AI era, it reinforces our positioning in ways a press release never will. The trust someone builds with an audience over years... it transfers. And recruiting. Honestly, the single most consistent source of great talent I've found is LinkedIn. People want to work for leaders they've been following. That's not theoretical. I've watched it happen.

So if you're managing people with real audiences and you're treating that as a liability or a distraction, I'd push back pretty hard on that.

## **On How You Actually Build One**

Okay, but "encourage your people to build a personal brand" is useless advice on its own. Everyone nods at that in the all-hands and then goes back to never posting. So let's get specific, because I think the "how" is where most of this falls apart.

**First, kill the idea that you need a system before you start.**I don't have a content calendar. I don't have a ghostwriter. I don't have some AI queue quietly pumping out posts on my behalf. I post when I actually have something to say, and I try to write it in a way that makes it worth someone's time to stop scrolling.

If you're waiting to build the perfect process before you post your first thing, you'll wait forever. Write what you'd tell a friend. The process can come later, if it comes at all.

**Second, get specific instead of vague.**Vague thought leadership is invisible. Nobody remembers "AI is changing marketing." People remember the exact story, the exact number, the exact moment that made you believe it. If you're coaching someone on your team through this, the fastest unlock isn't a writing tip, it's asking them "okay, but what actually happened?"

**Third, treat it like a conversation, not a presentation.** The posts and the sections that do nothing are the ones written like a press release. The ones that land are the ones that sound like you're talking to one specific person, not broadcasting to an audience.

**Fourth, don't be afraid of a sharper hook.**This one took me a while to accept. You can respect your reader and still earn the first three seconds of their attention. Those aren't in conflict.

**And fifth, consistency beats perfection, every time.**You don't need a framework to be consistent. You need to enjoy it enough that it becomes a habit instead of a chore.

That's the individual level. But if you're doing this across a team, there's one more layer.

**Pick two or three themes each person actually has the right to own, not just whatever's trending that week.** And commit to a cadence, even a loose one. Consistency is what separates insight from noise, and it's what separates leaders from participants. Without that structure, you end up with a team full of good instincts and nothing to show for it.

None of this requires a big program. It requires you to stop treating your people's voice like something to manage down, and start treating it like something worth building on purpose.

## **Don’t Be Bland as F*****

This is a copy from my LinkedIn post and subsequent article on[Pavilion’s Topline.](https://toplinemedia.substack.com/p/dont-be-bland-as-fck-why-ai-isnt?utm_source=www.therevenuediaries.com&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=revenue-diaries-entry-74)

Everyone has the same tools now. The only edge left is the one thing you can’t prompt into existence: taste.

## **Nobody’s Talking about Brand Anymore**

I know I risk our future AI gods reading this at some point and annihilating my entire family because of my opinion, but YOLO. Brand wins.

In every single demo, event, and conversation I’ve had recently about the evolution of GTM and AI, there was not one mention of brand. Not one mention of taste. Not one mention of the power of human-driven creativity.

Not one.

I’m not against AI. We’re building agentic workflows at [Docebo](https://www.docebo.com/?utm_source=www.therevenuediaries.com&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=revenue-diaries-entry-74). I spend more time in Claude than I do in most other tools. I believe AI transformation is real and that the companies that ignore it will pay for that choice.

But there’s a version of that transformation that terrifies me. The one where marketing gets reduced to a growth function, or even worse, a function that reports to sales or product. Optimized to scale and engineered to be bland as f*ck. Where the output is technically correct, statistically average, and completely forgettable.

If that’s where this is going, I’m out. You can call me old. You can call me traditional.

But I’m going to call the blind shift to all-out AI a mistake.

## **Humans as the Moat**

Every major technological shift in history has flattened execution and sharpened the importance of human judgment. The printing press democratized text. The internet democratized distribution. And AI is democratizing production.

When everyone has the same tools, the only competitive advantage you have left is the human.

But… not the human as a checkbox. And not as part of the approval workflow. The human as the source of something the machine literally cannot generate: genuine taste, genuine point of view, genuine creative courage.

That’s the moat. And most companies are bulldozing it.

## **Consensus Isn’t Quality**

I keep coming back to the same argument I had with Adam Singer: Most brands don’t have a compliance problem. No, their problem is lack of taste. They’ve mistaken consensus for quality. They’ve run their work through so many layers of approval that by the time it reaches the market, every edge has been sanded off. Adam calls it the “blandification” of marketing. I don’t have a better word for it.

The result is a market full of sameness. Same messaging structure. Same visual language. Same LinkedIn posts. Same event booths, same generic swag.

And now AI can replicate that sameness at 10x the speed.

Congratulations! We’ve successfully industrialized mediocrity.

## **“Brand vs. Demand” Is a Needless Distraction**

Drew Brucker put it simply when we talked on [my podcast](https://open.spotify.com/episode/0TqOBAMQV2YJ8hHlBAhkWX?utm_source=www.therevenuediaries.com&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=revenue-diaries-entry-74): “Brand is a controllable moat. Features can be copied. Ads can be outbid. But brand? It’s how you get on the shortlist. It’s how you get remembered.”

The irony is that most operators still roll their eyes at the word “brand,” even as they wonder why their win rates are dropping and their pipeline velocity is slowing.

Here’s what I’ve learned from 15 years of running marketing: the “brand vs. demand” debate is the dumbest argument in the building. They’re not two budget lines. Nor are they competing priorities. They’re the same investment, measured at different time horizons.

Take, for instance, an event: It drives pipeline, builds perception, and helps you to retain customers. It also creates content that runs for six months. Asking whether that’s “brand spend” or “demand spend” is a waste of time, because it’s both, and calling it one or the other is a distraction from the actual work.

Don’t screw around. The real question you should be asking your team: Do your customers believe you’re the best at what you do? And is that belief showing up in win rates, deal size, and retention?

If not, you don’t need more attribution software or a cool AI agent. You might need better taste.

## **Taste Is The One Thing That Doesn’t Have a Vendor.**

You can’t buy it. You can’t template it. You can’t prompt it into existence. It’s discipline, judgment, and the courage to make choices that most people in your building are too afraid to make.

I wrote the [10 Laws of Good Taste](https://www.therevenuediaries.com/p/revenue-diaries-entry-48) last year, and the one that keeps resonating: Taste isn’t decoration. It’s substance embedded in every single decision. It shows up in the event’s lighting, the copy on your landing page, the follow-up email after a customer call, the way your sales deck flows.

Anywhere there’s a decision, taste either shows up or it doesn’t. And when it doesn’t, your customers feel it. They can’t always pinpoint why, but they feel something is off. And “something is off” is not a place you can run a growth function from.

## **When Production Becomes Cheap and Fast, What Becomes Rare Is Creative Conviction.**

Who’s going to win in this race to the blandest? Not the organizations that automate the fastest! It’s those leaders who know what their company stands for clearly enough to make every automated output feel human. That requires a core narrative, and a real point of view. Someone willing to say “this is boring and we’re not shipping it,” even when the calendar says otherwise.

That’s a human job. It will always be a human job.

## **Protecting Taste Is the Job Now.**

Rick Rubin can’t play an instrument. But he’s produced some of the most iconic records of our time, because he knows what moving feels like and has the conviction to protect it. That skill doesn’t degrade in an AI world. It becomes more valuable.

I’m building AI into everything I do. My team runs AI Build Days. We’re deploying agents. We’re building faster than we ever have.

And I’m more convinced than ever that none of it matters if we don’t know what we’re saying, why it matters, and how it should feel to the people on the other side of it.

Because agentic efficiency in service of bland output is just fast mediocrity.

The most important thing a marketing leader can do right now is not figure out which AI tools to deploy, but instead, build a culture where taste is protected, creativity is defended, and the human voice inside the work is treated as a strategic asset, not an inefficiency to be optimized away.

Brand is not a budget line. It’s the last moat you have, and the humans are the ones who build it.

While machines will get faster, they will never get taste.

So don’t give yours away.

kept.blurb: Open rates can be misleading, with revenue serving as the stronger measure of email performance. Segment audiences by engagement, purchase frequency, and customer value to send more relevant campaigns. Increase frequency when subscribers are engaged, test different opt-in offers beyond discounts, and review automations for missed revenue. Instead of removing inactive subscribers, use reactivation campaigns to bring back customers who may still convert.

Title: Email Pro: Open Rate Is a Vanity Metric

URL Source: https://www.practicalecommerce.com/email-pro-open-rate-is-a-vanity-metric

Published Time: 2026-07-31T09:36:07+00:00

Markdown Content:
Nabeel Azeez runs a Dubai-based email marketing agency with clients in ecommerce, SaaS, and more. He emphasizes engagement-based segmentation and high frequency, sending for one client eight emails per day, each to a unique segment.

In our recent conversation, he shared his methods for driving revenue from ecommerce emails, including unorthodox views such as the open rate is a vanity metric and never unsubscribe dormant recipients.

Our entire audio is embedded below. The transcript is edited for clarity and length.

**Eric Bandholz:** What do you do?

**Nabeel Azeez:** I’m the co-owner of Dropkick Copy, an email marketing agency in Dubai. We work with pretty much every kind of business — ecommerce, SaaS, private equity, et cetera.

Nearly all of our clients are in the United States.

**Bandholz:** What is your roadmap for onboarding clients?

**Azeez:** Assume it’s a B2B company. The first thing we do is send a nine-word email to all the subscribers who haven’t bought anything. The aim is to get people to raise their hands. We ask them, “Are you still interested in what we’re selling?”

We typically get a few hundred responses, depending on the list.

For ecommerce clients, we check which flows they’re missing and install them. Then we up the frequency.

Most ecommerce brands send around three emails per week. We’ll increase it to daily, sometimes several per day, depending on their segments. For one ecommerce client, we send upwards of eight emails per day, each to a different segment.

We’re aggressive. [Klaviyo](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/klaviyo-founder-were-good-at-storing-data) sent us a warning the other day stating we’re emailing too many unengaged subscribers. But Klaviyo ought to know that open rate is a vanity metric. The only thing that matters is revenue.

**Bandholz:** How do you build the eight segments?

**Azeez:** So the easiest way is by engagement — the last seven days, 30 days, or 60 to 90 days. Another segment consists of folks who subscribed long ago but haven’t engaged recently.

Then we segment the “whales,” subscribers who buy often and spend a lot. “Potential whales,” another segment, buy often but don’t spend as much as the whales. Another is loyal customers, who buy frequently in smaller amounts.

We also look for whales who are about to churn or haven’t bought in a long time. We call them “churned whales” or “lapsed whales.”

In other words, you can split up your customer or subscriber list into many different segments. There’s no overlap. It’s one email per person.

The messaging and strategy depend on the segment. Take a potential whale, somebody who buys often but in lesser order sizes than a whale. We incentivize potential whales to spend more per order by offering a gift for minimum order values.

Another option is to send the exact email to all segments but personalize it. Klaviyo has a dynamic content selector to insert the message based on a segment or a custom subscriber field.

**Bandholz:** Say I’m a smaller brand with $10,000 in monthly email revenue. I’m sending three times per week to basic segments. I’ve set up simple flows, such as post-purchase and abandoned carts. How can I grow from $10,000 to $20,000?

**Azeez:** First, it depends on your products. Are they repeat, consumable items or one-offs? Second, how many subscribers are you adding every week? The more new subscribers you have, the more aggressively you can email them.

Plus, some merchants don’t care about long-term subscribers. We’re much more aggressive with those audiences than with brands seeking ongoing relationships.

But I would at least go from three times per week to daily emails, as long as the list is growing. I would also review your email automations for missed revenue opportunities.

It’s important, too, to know how your email affects performance on other channels. A solid email program can drive ROAS and MER on Meta Ads, for example. Switch email attribution from last-click to first-click for the metrics.

**Bandholz:** What are common [email marketing](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/category/marketing/email) mistakes of ecommerce companies?

**Azeez:** Merchants don’t test their opt-in pop-up offers enough. That includes removing the pop-up completely and tracking margins. Offering a 10% discount trains shoppers to expect it in other promotions.

Experiment with the best offer to entice new subscribers. Is it a discount, a free product, or free shipping? Perhaps it’s a bundle of related items.

**Bandholz:** What is the best way to phase out unengaged subscribers?

**Azeez:** Set up a [sunset unengaged automation](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/rethink-your-email-sunset-policy). I typically set it to 90 days. If they haven’t opened, clicked, or purchased within the past 90 days, they will receive that automated message. If they still show no signs of life, we’ll pause them for a while.

I try not to unsubscribe them. I’ll keep them and send a reactivation email every month or quarter. In my experience, around 10% of unengaged folks will come back eventually.

Our reactivation emails look like other emails, though we’ll occasionally send a plain-text version to spur a response. Sometimes we send long, educational, text-only messages that are much more likely to land in the main inbox than a promotion.

**Bandholz:** How do you use SMS?

**Azeez:** We try to send the same volume of [SMS messages](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/rcs-or-sms-it-depends-on-the-task) as email unless it’s daily. We won’t send daily SMSs, but we’ll try two or three times a week. Again, it depends on the brand. SMS usually makes a lot more money than email. So we’ll bump up SMSs if we need more revenue.

A promotional SMS should be as short as possible. It also depends on the cost. Sending SMSs is typically more expensive than emails.

**Bandholz:** Where can people follow you, reach out to you, buy your services?

**Azeez:** Our agency’s site is [DropkickCopy.com](https://www.dropkickcopy.com/). My own site is [Nabeelazeez.com](https://www.nabeelazeez.com/). I’m [@NabeelAzeez](https://x.com/nabeelazeez?lang=en) on X.

kept.heading: GOOGLE PUBLISHES ITS FIRST DEDICATED GUIDE FOR YOUTUBE AUDIO ADS (2 MINUTE READ)

kept.article_text:
Title: Create YouTube audio ads - Google Ads Help

URL Source: https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/10227746

Markdown Content:
YouTube audio ads allow you to tap into audiences who are listening to music, podcasts, or other audio content on YouTube. Using YouTube audio ads, you can expand your reach and increase brand awareness for your target audience.

#### View audio ads in action

Select a button to view an example of a YouTube audio ad.

**Simple animation**:

[Video 5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_t6UAuvLKFs)

**Static image**:

[Video 6](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mLNgjvHG4RE)

To view subtitles in your language, [turn on YouTube captions](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/100078). Select the Settings icon ![Image 1: Image of YouTube settings icon](https://storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/UrHzzlx74G5ig5vYXo9Nk43r7NM5fj72Tbu1) at the top right corner of the video player, select "Captions," and then specify your language.

* * *

## Benefits

*   **Efficient reach**: Extends reach of video campaigns into new inventory at a low cost.
*   **Simplified buying**: Buying and campaign setup is the same as other YouTube ad formats.
*   **Streamlined targeting and measurement features**: Use advanced audiences, get access to the latest version of Brand Lift measurement, and view your reporting in Google Ads.
*   **Lower creative production costs**: Audio ads are often less expensive to produce than video ads, as the recommended visual component is a still image or a simple animation.

## Audio inventory on YouTube

Reach users with an audio optimized ad when users are on audio surfaces and in listening-first states on both YouTube and YouTube Music.

## Creative specifications

| **Required asset file** | A link to your YouTube video ([make sure to upload the video to YouTube](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/57407)) |
| --- |
| **Ad length & Serving Types** | **Maximum**: 30 seconds **Note**: Creatives up to 15 seconds will be served as a non-skippable ad and creatives 16-30 seconds will be served as a skippable ad. |
| **File size** | **Maximum**: 128GB |
| **Resolution** | 426 x 240 (240p) 640 x 360 (360p) 854 x 480 (480p) 1280 x 720 (720p) 1920 x 1080 (1080p) 2560 x 1440 (1440p) 3840 x 2160 (2160p) |
| **Aspect ratio** | 16:9 (if 4:3, black bars are added on the sides of the image or animation) |

## Best practices

YouTube audio ads run during long listening sessions and when YouTube is playing in the background. Use these best practices when you create the ad.

*   Introduce your business or product early and focus on the key message you want the audience takeaway with.
*   **Focus on sound**: YouTube audio ads should focus on the audio component, so use assets with light animation or a static image with a call-to-action. Make sure to upload your creative as a YouTube URL.
*   **Have a consistent tone and tempo**: For a 30 second ad, aim for 60-80 words when using a voiceover in the ad.
*   **Be conversational**: A friendly tone helps transition listeners between entertainment content and ads.
*   **Include a call-to-action in the audio or in the video creative**: Offer an opportunity for listeners to take the next step, such as reading or showing a short link to your website in the ad.
*   **Comply with our policies**: Ads shouldn’t be overly intrusive to listeners, so make sure to [comply with the Google Ads policies](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/6008942).

## Instructions

1.   In your Google Ads account, click the **Campaigns**icon ![Image 2: Campaigns Icon](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/PYU3UjHzepAdY-dWS9ObIzq9WgLGS0SZeJS1hQ0Be3fxCIUQZaWCrR4HoYqriXSEbQ=w40).
2.   Click the **Campaigns**drop down in the section menu, then select **[Campaigns](https://ads.google.com/aw/campaigns)**.
3.   Click the plus button ![Image 3](https://storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/Ns5o4jgOAKaw8NnTPog3UMQHzmGiCUG3utl0) , then select **New campaign**.
4.   Select the **Brand awareness and reach** goal.
5.   Select the **Video** campaign type.
6.   Select **Audio** as your campaign subtype.
7.   Click **Continue**.
8.   Enter details about your campaign, such as the bid and the budget.
9.   Add targeting to your ad group. For optimal results, make sure that your targeting isn’t too narrow.
10.   Use the editor to add the URL for the YouTube video and then edit your ad’s copy.
11.   Set your Target CPM bid amount. Check the "Campaign estimates" widget to view an estimate on the available impressions and estimated performance. The estimated performance is a combination of targeting, budget, and bids. You can adjust your campaign settings to achieve your desired result. Keep in mind that if your bid is too low, your campaign may not perform well in the [Google Ads auction](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6366577) and you may not spend your full budget. Estimates are only provided when you’re using one ad format in your campaign. 
12.   When you finish, click **Create campaign**.

kept.heading: THE TOKEN PRICE COLLAPSE AND WHY AI COSTS STILL INCREASE (4 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Cheaper tokens didn't shrink AI bills - they multiplied how many calls get made. Token prices fell more than 95% in three years, yet enterprise LLM spend more than doubled in 6 months to $8.4 billion. The volume surge lands directly on margin, since AI-native gross margins run 50-60% against 80-90% for traditional per-seat SaaS, and a flat seat price can't absorb a cost that scales with usage. That's forcing a shift toward per-action and per-outcome pricing, the model Salesforce, Intercom, and GitHub Copilot have already adopted.

Title: Token Price Collapse: Why AI Costs Still Keep Rising

URL Source: https://thegtmnewsletter.substack.com/p/ai-token-price-collapse-costs-rising

Published Time: 2026-07-31T23:52:48+00:00

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!x67_!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe3b58736-f77b-485f-842f-69b0b7224373_1752x658.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!x67_!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe3b58736-f77b-485f-842f-69b0b7224373_1752x658.png)

This week has showcased the continuous battle of competitors driving down the price of tokens.

First, OpenAI announced cost reduction to models GPT-5.6 Luna and GPT-5.6 Terra.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!YcO8!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7cd551a0-28c7-4daa-adca-bea069123b37_651x379.png)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/sarah-friar_starting-yesterday-gpt-56-luna-our-fastest-share-7488951573369458688-fNmb/?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop&rcm=ACoAAB-zOXwB7j95XB6LBuQURXJ8m_cTOBDTz_U)

The same day, DeepSeek dropped V4-Flash - an open model that competes on price too, and free to self-host.

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!7WCy!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2b7a85da-17bc-4e15-9f86-6031874ec29f_644x740.png)](https://x.com/deepseek_ai/status/2083084415157022911?s=20)

The chart below shows how popular models compare on cost. Artificial Analysis plots each one by its weighted average cost, in dollars, to run a single task on its Intelligence Index - lower is better.

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZiCf!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbeb7f664-39d8-4d33-9e8d-39e48ed6aa47_1095x619.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZiCf!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbeb7f664-39d8-4d33-9e8d-39e48ed6aa47_1095x619.png)

This is big news because DeepSeek’s model is approaching the same performance level as Opus 4.8, but for a fraction of the cost. The same task costs $0.03 on DeepSeek’s V4 Flash and $3.15 on Claude Fable 5.

Competition between different labs is pushing the price point down.

And this all just happened this week. If we zoom out, the price of an AI token fell by more than 95% in three years.

But for most companies, the AI bill went up anyway.

OpenAI’s flagship was launched at $30 per million input tokens in March 2023. By late 2024, DeepSeek V3 shipped frontier-class output at $0.14, roughly one hundredth of that. Google now processes over 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month, up from 9.7 trillion two years ago, and the per-token price dropped the entire way.

So the model has continuously gotten less expensive. The line item for companies has not. Enterprise spend on large language models more than doubled in six months, from $3.5 billion in late 2024 to $8.4 billion by mid-2025 (Menlo research). Prices fell about 10x. Consumption rose far faster.

Two numbers get quoted all the time - they point in opposite directions and both are true:

1.   The price per token. Hold quality steady, and it’s collapsed.

2.   The volume of tokens we’re burning. It’s exploded past the price drop.

Hold quality steady, and the price of a token has collapsed. Look at how much teams actually buy, and usage has blown right past it.

Google is the cleanest proof, because they showed both sides. At I/O 2026, Sundar Pichai said Google went from 9.7 trillion tokens a month to over 3.2 quadrillion in two years. That’s about a 330x jump. Over the same stretch, the cost of GPT-4-level quality fell from $30 per million tokens to under $0.50.

This isn’t new, it’s the oldest pattern in tech. When a better steam engine cut the coal needed per job, total coal use went up, not down. Cheaper steam just made it worth using for a lot more jobs.

Cheap tokens did the same thing to AI. The second a call got cheap enough, teams started making a hundred of them where they used to make one.

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!bC77!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6df8646e-9ef3-453d-bdda-872c78136389_2048x1172.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!bC77!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6df8646e-9ef3-453d-bdda-872c78136389_2048x1172.png)

This is where the token context impacts go-to-market.

In classic SaaS, a common pricing model was _per seat,_ and the cost to serve one more user is often marginal. There’s still a cost of goods — hosting, storage, support — but it’s mostly fixed. It barely moves whether someone logs in once a month or a thousand times. That’s why software runs at 80-90% gross margin.

AI changes the shape of that cost. Every call burns tokens, and that’s a variable charge that grows with usage. Use the product twice as much, and that slice of COGS roughly doubles. There’s no “already paid for it.”

The numbers show it. Bessemer puts AI-native gross margins at 50 to 60%, against 80 to 90% for traditional SaaS. ICONIQ surveyed around 300 companies and pegged the average AI product margin at 52%, up from 41% two years ago. Two things follow.

First, the gap is closing on its own. As token prices fall, the same product earns more per dollar of revenue every quarter, without changing a thing.

Second, and this is the bigger one: a flat per-seat price can’t cover a variable per-call cost. Bolt an AI assistant onto an $80 seat, and inference can eat up quite a bit of margin.

That’s why seat pricing is breaking. The pricing model is now the lever that decides who keeps their margin.

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!vs4R!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb98bd950-4b6a-4776-8fef-960c32747c6c_2048x1198.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!vs4R!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb98bd950-4b6a-4776-8fef-960c32747c6c_2048x1198.png)

When a team’s AI spend triples, the token price is almost never the reason.

It’s usually one of four habits. Each one has a real number behind it.

1.   Sending trivial work to the flagship model, at up to 50x the cost of a smaller one that could’ve done the job.

2.   Agents that loop with no budget. One four-agent system looped for eleven days and burned $47,000 before anyone caught it. The dashboards looked healthy the whole time. Bloated context, re-sent on every step. The conversation grows, and the cost grows with the square of it.

3.   No caching. Turn it on, and repeated input can run up to 90% cheaper.

The pattern underneath all four is the same.

The model isn’t necessarily expensive, the way it’s being used is.

The teams holding their margin do two things. They treat tokens like a real cost of goods. Then they pass that cost to the customer through pricing.

It starts with visibility. Tag every call by team and feature, so tokens show up as a COGS line you can actually see. You can’t cut what you can’t measure. From there, four moves on the cost side.

1.   Route every call to the smallest model that can do the job. That alone cuts 40 to 85% of spend. Coinbase nearly halved its bill this way, and usage kept growing the whole time.

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!xbME!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3c61226c-b9f9-45f7-aa6a-dcd07d45b1df_824x164.png)](https://thenewstack.io/multi-model-ai-infrastructure/)

1.   Cache aggressively. Repeated input runs up to 90% cheaper.

2.   Cap hard. Set limits that actually stop an agent, not alerts that tell you after the money’s gone. A hard cap is what kills a $47,000 loop on day one.

3.   Trim your context. Don’t re-send the whole conversation on every step. Cap the history, summarize old turns, and the cost stops growing with the square of the thread.

Then one move on the revenue side: reprice for the outcome. Put the variable cost on the customer, not your margin.

Title: Ends Tonight? How False Urgency Became Email’s $500 Per Subscriber Mistake | Martech Zone

URL Source: https://martech.zone/ends-tonight-how-false-urgency-became-emails-500-per-subscriber-mistake/

Published Time: 2026-08-01T08:47:52-04:00

Markdown Content:
![Image 1: Ends Tonight? How False Urgency Became Email’s $500 per Subscriber Mistake](https://martech.zone/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/fales-email-subject-line-cema-liability-420x236.webp)

Scarcity sells. Decades of behavioral research, from [Robert Cialdini’s principles of persuasion](https://refer.martech.zone/book/robert-cialdini/influence/) onward, confirm what merchants have known forever: people act faster when they believe an opportunity is about to disappear. Modern marketing turned that instinct into infrastructure. Countdown timers, low-stock badges, flash sales, and deadline-driven subject lines are not fringe tactics; they are the default settings of the promotional calendar.

The engine behind all of it is **Fear Of Missing Out ([FOMO](https://martech.zone/acronym/fomo/))**, and it works precisely because the audience believes the clock is real. That belief is now being tested in court, and the results should change how every email team in the United States writes a subject line.

## The $500 Subject Line

Washington State’s **Commercial Electronic Mail Act ([CEMA](https://martech.zone/acronym/cema/))** has prohibited commercial email containing false or misleading information in the subject line since 1998. For most of its life, the law chased actual spammers. That ended on April 17, 2025, when the Washington Supreme Court ruled that the statute means what it says:

> A _ny_ false or misleading information in a subject line violates the law, not just deception about who sent the message.
> 
> [Brown v. Old Navy](https://www.courts.wa.gov/opinions/pdf/1025921.pdf)

The injury is simply _receiving_ the email. No one needs to have opened it, believed it, or bought anything.

The numbers attached to that ruling explain everything that followed. CEMA at the time provided statutory damages of **$500 per email**, per recipient, with no cap and no requirement to prove harm. Each violation is also automatically an unfair or deceptive practice under Washington’s **Consumer Protection Act ([CPA](https://martech.zone/acronym/cpa-5/))**, which adds attorney fees and the possibility of trebled damages.

A single national campaign touching a few hundred thousand Washington inboxes carries theoretical exposure in the hundreds of millions of dollars. Within a year of the Brown decision, plaintiffs’ firms had filed [more than 100 CEMA class actions](https://www.ballardspahr.com/insights/alerts-and-articles/2026/04/cema-ingly-endless-litigation-brown-v-old-navy-turns-1-year-old), a total that grew to nearly 200 against retailers, airlines, hotels, colleges, insurers, and beauty brands. One detail from that litigation deserves its own sentence: not a single plaintiff claims to have actually read the challenged emails.

## The Brands in the Crosshairs

The defendant list reads like a mall directory, but a handful of cases define the trend and its trajectory:

**Brand****Case and Venue****What the Emails Said****Where It Stands**
Old Navy Brown v. Old Navy, certified to the Washington Supreme Court Time-limited sale subject lines for promotions that kept running April 2025 ruling: any false or misleading subject line is actionable; litigation continues
Nike Ma v. Nike, King County, removed to the Western District of Washington _Only a few hours left

Ends tonight

Last chance to save an extra 25%_ Court rejected Nike’s federal preemption defense in January 2026; ongoing
Tommy Bahama Haley v. Tommy Bahama, King County _Ends Tonight!

Limited Time Only_ Filed late 2025; ongoing
Macy’s Western District of Washington _Open ASAP: up to 65% off ends tomorrow_ Filed November 2025; ongoing
Costco Class action on behalf of Washington residents _Today is the last day to access Member-Only Saving

Hot Buys available for 5 Days Only_$14 million settlement, preliminary approval June 23, 2026; claims due August 24, 2026

A necessary clarification before going further: none of these companies has been found guilty of anything. These are _civil_ claims, and Costco’s settlement, like most, involves no admission of wrongdoing. What has actually been decided is the legal architecture around the claims, and every one of those decisions has gone against the marketers.

The [Nike](https://refer.martech.zone/nike/) case shows how. Filed in May 2025 over [subject lines implying sales were about to expire](https://www.classaction.org/news/nike-hit-with-class-action-lawsuit-in-washington-over-marketing-emails) when the promotions were extended or never time-limited at all, the case produced a January 14, 2026 ruling that the federal **CAN-SPAM Act ([CAN-SPAM](https://martech.zone/acronym/can-spam/))**[does not preempt CEMA’s subject line provision](https://www.faegredrinker.com/en/insights/publications/2026/1/federal-court-upholds-washington-state-commercial-electronic-mail-act-against-can-spam-preemption-argument). Congress preempted state email laws in 2003 but explicitly spared statutes that prohibit falsity or deception, and district courts have uniformly rejected the preemption defense since then. The federal law marketers actually comply with offers no shield against the state law they have never heard of.

The [Tommy Bahama complaint](https://emailexpert.com/industry-news/tommy-bahama-faces-cema-lawsuit-over-ends-tonight-email-subject-lines/) is nearly identical in theory, and the [Costco settlement](https://www.classaction.org/news/14m-costco-settlement-resolves-class-action-lawsuit-over-promo-emails-with-allegedly-misleading-subject-lines) shows where the road leads. Costco agreed to pay $14 million to Washington residents who received its marketing email between June 2021 and July 2026, with individual payments of up to $500, after a complaint alleged the company advertised time-limited promotions it knew it would extend. It is the first headline number in the wave and the benchmark every pending defendant now negotiates against. Courts have not yet awarded damages at trial in any of these cases, so settlements are, for now, where the real penalties are being set.

## Email Is the Forensic Surface of Marketing

The sharpest framing of why this is happening to email, rather than to the identical urgency copy running on television and shelf wobblers, comes from [Dela Quist](https://www.linkedin.com/in/delaquist/), the founder of Alchemy Worx and one of email marketing’s most influential strategic voices. In a December 2025 LinkedIn post written as the Tommy Bahama suit landed, he argued that asking why email keeps ending up in court is the wrong question. The better one:

> Why is email the only channel that gets caught?
> 
> [Dela Quist](https://www.linkedin.com/in/delaquist/)

His answer is structural. Every email carries a permanent, searchable, admissible record of exactly what was claimed, to whom, and when. Channel-specific statutes like CEMA give plaintiffs a precise legal hook that broadcast and in-store promotions lack. The same message hitting millions of inboxes creates perfect class action conditions, because if one line misled anyone, it allegedly misled everyone identically. And email marketers face double exposure, liable under both email-specific laws and general consumer protection statutes. A sale sign that stays up an extra day is unprovable; an email is its own receipt, metadata included.

> Email isn’t being singled out because it’s worse. It’s being singled out because it’s traceable, testable, and codified. It’s the forensic surface of marketing.
> 
> [Dela Quist](https://www.linkedin.com/in/delaquist/)

Or, as he compressed it:

> TV implies urgency. Shelf wobblers suggest urgency. Email documents it.
> 
> [Dela Quist](https://www.linkedin.com/in/delaquist/)

## What Changed in June 2026

The litigation wave got Olympia’s attention. Governor Bob Ferguson signed House Bill 2274 on March 23, 2026, and the [amended CEMA took effect June 11, 2026](https://www.morganlewis.com/pubs/2026/06/washington-legislature-narrows-state-anti-spam-law-after-retail-litigation-surge). Statutory damages for subject line violations dropped from $500 to $100 per email, and plaintiffs must now show the sender had actual knowledge, or knowledge fairly implied from the circumstances, that the subject line was false or misleading when it was sent.

Read the fine print before relaxing. The amendment is not retroactive, so the nearly 200 cases filed before June 11 proceed under the old $500 framework, and plaintiffs raced to meet the filing deadline. The Consumer Protection Act hook survives intact, including attorney fees. And $100 per email, per recipient, across a Washington-sized slice of a national list, still multiplies into eight figures fast. The legislature installed a speed bump, not a roadblock.

## Why This Matters Far Beyond Washington

It is tempting to file this under regional trivia. That would be a mistake, for four reasons.

*   **You cannot geo-fence an email list:** no **Email Service Provider ([ESP](https://martech.zone/acronym/esp/))** segment reliably excludes Washington’s eight million residents, and CEMA applies when a sender has reason to know a recipient lives there, a standard plaintiffs meet with the signup data already sitting in your own platform.
*   **Federal compliance is not a defense:** courts have uniformly held CAN-SPAM does not preempt deception-based state laws, so a fully CAN-SPAM-compliant program remains fully exposed.
*   **The playbook is portable:** other states have their own anti-spam and consumer protection statutes with the same falsity carve-out, and the plaintiffs’ bar has now proven the economics.
*   **The evidence is permanent:** every campaign you have ever sent is already archived in millions of inboxes, discoverable years after the send date. Your exposure is not prospective; it is sitting in Sent folders.

Any US company that emails consumers, anywhere, should treat Washington’s standard as the national standard, because functionally it already is.

## Are Your Subject Lines a Liability?

The good news buried in all of this is that urgency is not illegal. **False urgency**is. The audit that separates the two takes an afternoon, and these are the questions to ask:

*   **Does the deadline exist?** If the subject line says the sale ends tonight, it must end tonight and stay ended. Extending a promotion after an urgency send is the core fact pattern in nearly every one of these lawsuits.
*   **Is the discount real?** Percentage-off claims measured against inflated list prices that nothing ever sells for make the subject line misleading even when the deadline is genuine.
*   **Does the subject line match the offer?** Free products that require a purchase, sitewide sales with sweeping exclusions, and last-chance framing for offers that recur weekly all create a gap between the promise and the landing page.
*   **What is your automation saying?** Evergreen journeys, resend-to-non-opener flows, and recycled templates repeat final hours language on autopilot. Audit what the system sends, not just what the calendar plans.
*   **Can you prove it?** Keep a record of every promotion’s advertised start, end, and terms. If a claim arrives, documentation showing the sale ended exactly as promised is the entire defense.
*   **Who signs off?** Subject line review cannot stop at brand voice and open-rate instinct. Someone with authority needs to check every urgency claim against operational reality before the send.

If any answer makes you wince, you are not being edgy; you are incurring statutory damages equal to your Washington list size per send.

## Urgency Without the Lie

There is a strategic upside hiding in the compliance work. Manufactured urgency is a depreciating asset: audiences learn quickly that your deadlines are decorative, and every extended _final hours_ sale teaches subscribers to ignore the next one. Real deadlines, honestly enforced, are what make FOMO work in the first place.

The brands that treat accountability as a constraint will keep feeding the plaintiffs’ bar. The ones that treat it the way Dela Quist frames it, as the defining structural property of the channel, will end up with the only urgency messaging that still converts: the kind that is true.

## AI shopping went mainstream faster than any channel before it. Here are the numbers you need to know about where it is and where it's going.

Published on July 28, 2026 • Last updated on July 28, 2026 • 5 minutes read

### Spy on Any Website

Get traffic data and keyword intel on competitors instantly.

AI has become a mainstream shopping research tool faster than any channel that came before it. Here’s the data that matters for marketers and that can help you make arguments for getting your organization AI-ready. The following stats are drawn exclusively from reports published in 2026 and are organized by what each tells us about how consumers and business buyers use AI chatbots and agents to inform purchases.

## Adoption

*   43% of U.S. online shoppers used an AI assistant — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity, or a comparable tool — for product research in the past 90 days. Among them, 20% used AI on their most recent online purchase over $50. ([Product.ai](https://product.ai/research/trust-in-ai-commerce-report/))

![Image 1: Image 14](https://martech.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/image-14-800x600.png.webp)
*   1 in 4 customers already turn to AI-powered platforms as their primary source when searching for information, making purchase decisions or finding recommendations — surpassing brand websites and online reviews. ([Adobe](https://business.adobe.com/resources/digital-trends-report.html))
*   24% of non-adopters cite preference for familiar sources as the top reason for not using AI for shopping; 17% cite lack of trust. Bad experiences rank last at 4%. ([L.E.K. Consulting](https://www.lek.com/insights/consumer-products/thanks-ai-consumers-are-arriving-brand-and-retailer-sites-ready-buy))
*   30% of all U.S. consumers have used AI tools to inform a purchase decision — adoption that’s spread across generations but skews younger: 40% of Gen Z, 42% of millennials, 28% of Gen X, and 13% of baby boomers. (L.E.K. Consulting)
*   AI adoption for product research declines sharply after age 44 (Product.ai).

![Image 2: Image 40](https://martech.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/image-40-800x329.png.webp)

## Where AI fits in the purchase funnel

*   46% of AI users now start their purchase research on a stand-alone AI platform (ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Claude), up from 25% in 2024, while traditional search fell from 43% to 24% over the same period. (L.E.K. Consulting)
*   53% of AI users primarily use it to compare options and narrow a short list, ahead of final decision-making (21%), and discovery (19%). (L.E.K. Consulting)
*   49% of customers would use AI to search for personalized product recommendations; 44% would use it for instant customer service. (Adobe)

## Trust and the verification gap

*   86% of U.S. shoppers who used AI for product research verified the AI’s recommendation through another source before buying. (Product.ai)
*   AI tools ranked sixth on a list of most-trusted product information sources, behind (in order): Family and friends, online customer reviews, expert publications or professionals, brand/retailer websites, Reddit/online forums, and ahead of only YouTube creators/reviewers. (Product.ai)
*   42% of shoppers would trust AI for a purchase under $50 without checking another source first. Only 5% would trust it for a purchase over $500. (Product.ai)
*   66% of AI adopters believe AI provides accurate results, and 85% say it improved their shopping experience overall. (L.E.K. Consulting)
*   68% of organizations say clear disclosure of AI interactions is the most important trust-building factor for agentic AI; 61% say easy escalation to human support. (Adobe)

## The traffic impact

*   1,200% year-over-year surge in AI-sourced traffic to U.S. retail websites. AI-referred shoppers convert at 31% higher rates than those arriving from other sources. (Adobe)
*   176% compound annual growth rate for AI-referred web traffic, while search, social, and direct traffic remains flat. (L.E.K. Consulting)
*   More than 1.1 billion retail site visits a month came from AI in 2025 — a 357% year-over-year increase. (L.E.K. Consulting)
*   62% of consumers across the U.S., EMEA, and Asia-Pacific have used AI to inform where they go next in their shopping journey. (L.E.K. Consulting)
*   Agentic shoppers could account for $190 billion to $385 billion in U.S. ecommerce spending by 2030, capturing 10% to 20% of total online retail sales. ([NielsenIQ](https://nielseniq.com/global/en/insights/report/2026/commerce-trends-intelligence/))

## Category breakdown: Where AI research matters most

*   71% of consumers use AI for travel research, 65% for consumer electronics, and 62% for financial products. No category tracked falls below 47%. (L.E.K. Consulting)
*   Apparel accounts for 30% of shoppers’ most recent AI-researched purchases over $50, the largest single category; electronics accounts for 20%. (Product.ai)

## The pre-decided shopper

*   31% of AI users say their purchase decision was largely made before they reached a brand or retailer site, up from 26% two years ago. (L.E.K. Consulting)
*   Average web visit duration fell 6% overall across 13 categories tracked between March 2024 and March 2026, with the steepest drops in household essentials (18%), healthcare services (16%), and beauty and personal care (16%). (L.E.K. Consulting)

## Consumer sentiment toward agentic AI

*   47% of customers would be comfortable having their personal AI agent work with a brand’s human representative. Fewer would let their agent work with a brand’s AI agent, hand over personal information, or authorize a purchase. (Adobe)
*   40% of customers haven’t even considered creating a personal AI agent. (Adobe)
*   Just over half of consumers are open to AI tools that help them find coupons and deals; far fewer are comfortable with AI handling transactions on their behalf. ([Gartner](https://www.gartner.com/en/documents/7521153))
*   57% of consumers prefer physical stores. (Gartner)
